Claim No: 2225465/2024 5. Miss Bibi confirmed that the email should have referred to the 2010 Act, noting that there was no similar 2006 Act. 6. I informed the Claimant that the Respondent had complied with the Tribunal’s case management order and served its position statement on the date required by the agreed extension. As disability was contested, I would be determining the issue today and I therefore would not be granting the Claimant’s application to bar the Respondent from contesting disability. 7. The Claimant’s second concern was that the Respondent had twice requested extensions to the date for filing an amended response after the first case management hearing. It was clarified with Ms Bibi that the amended Grounds of Resistance were filed and sent to the Claimant on 30 April 2025, the date agreed by the Tribunal upon the Respondent’s second request for an extension of time. Whist the document appears to have been filed after 6pm, there was no time specified by the Tribunal and as such I could not say that the Respondent had failed to file the amended response in line with the extension granted. I would not be making a finding that the Respondent had failed to comply with an order. 8. The Claimant confirmed that the reasonable adjustments he had requested related to this hearing, not the final hearing. He was given additional time to answer questions, permitted to screen share a document and given the time he needed to prepare of each part of the hearing in line with the requests he had made. Disability status 9. Having heard submissions from the parties as to whether the Claimant had proved (the burden being on him) that he was a disabled person in accordance with section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024 (when the disciplinary proceedings took place) I determined that he was not. 10. In accordance with Wigginton v Cowie and ors t/a Baxter International (A Partnership) EAT 0322/09 I asked myself four questions in sequential order: • did the claimant have a mental and/or physical impairment? (the ‘impairment condition’) • did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out normal dayto-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) • was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial condition’), and • was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’). Claim No: 2225465/2024 11. The burden of proving disability rested on the Claimant. He had supplied an impact statement, however that was not supported by the medical records (nor was there any other evidence, such as Personal Independence Payments or similar). 12. I had regard to the judgment of His Honour Judge Auerbach in Igweike v TSB Bank plc: ‘[I]t is a practical fact that, in some cases of this type, the individual’s own evidence may not be sufficient to satisfy the tribunal of the existence of an impairment... The question is a purely practical or evidential one, which is sensitive to the nature of the alleged disability, the facts, and the nature of the evidence, in the given case.’ Question 1 - Did the Claimant have a mental or physical impairment at the date he was undergoing disciplinary proceedings? 13. The Claimant saw a doctor for the first time on 5 August 2024 and was signed off for 2 weeks, 1 – 15 August 2024, having cited stress at work and anxiety. No detail was given as to functional effects of condition on certificate. The doctor’s note of 5 August states that the Claimant reported that he had been under lot of stress working under difficult manager. He said he had been suspended, the doctor records the reason was unknown (although the Claimant had already attended the investigation interview). The Claimant reported that he missed a disciplinary hearing the previous Thursday. He had not been back at work since then but was planning to file a dispute. The doctor recorded that a long conversation took place about the situation at work. The doctor concluded “Emotionally not acutely distressed”. He “agreed” to issue a certificate for 2 weeks. 14. Prev note is dated 23 July 24 when a reminder was sent that the Claimant was due an NHS health check. There are no earlier records where the Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his disability impact statement such as poor sleep, difficulty with personal care and household tasks. 15. I find that first presentation with work related stress was 5 August 2024 and that the stress complained of was due to disciplinary process at work. This could be considered a mental impairment. Question 2 - Did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 16. The consultation on 5 August 2024 does not suggest an adverse impact on day to day activities. 17. Whilst the Claimant has provided an impact statement, according to which his symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting his role with the Co-op in October 2023, there was no evidence whatsoever to support this assertion. Claim No: 2225465/2024 18. I find that had the Claimant suffered with difficulty with sleep and concentration, and an inability to care for himself from late 2023/early 2024 as asserts, he would have consulted his GP. He did not. I make this finding in part because he has been keen to seek assistance from September/October 2024, albeit that the records do not suggest a condition that adversely impacts on his day to day activities. Question 3 - Was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial condition’) 19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 2024 – the time he needs to establish disability). Question 4 - Was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’) 20. At the date of the disciplinary (12 August 2024 after 2 postponements because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with Boyle v SCA Packaging Ltd. I also take into account that how long an impairment is likely to last is something to be determined at the date of the alleged discriminatory act in accordance with McDougall v Richmond Adult Community Centre. Given the Claimant had not complained of any difficulties with day to day activities or even stress before he was told he was to attend a disciplinary hearing, I find that the likelihood was that any symptoms would resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded. 21. It follows that I do not find that the Claimant had a disability as defined in section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024, when the disciplinary process took place. Reasonable Adjustment complaint 22. The Claimant’s reasonable adjustment claim, which is dependent on him proving disability, is that he was required to attend a disciplinary hearing when he had been signed off as unfit for work. I therefore dismiss this claim. It has no reasonable prospects of success and cannot logically proceed in light of my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person. A separate judgment is issued accordingly. List of issues Claim No: 2225465/2024 23. The remaining issues in the claim, having made that decision are direct discrimination, victimisation and wrongful dismissal as set out below. This is the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines otherwise. Deposit Order 24. Having discussed the merits of the issues with the parties, I proposed, of my own volition, to make a deposit order, as set out in rule 40 of the Employment Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024. Having heard submissions, I made such an order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential liability for the Respondent’s costs. Claimant’s application for specific disclosure 25. The Claimant wrote to the Tribunal on 9 April 2025 requesting specific disclosure. He asked me to deal with that application. I did so, finding that the majority of the requests were not for documents relevant to the remaining issues in the claim (the Claimant’s unfair dismissal claim having previously been withdrawn due to lack of two years’ service). 26. I ordered that the Respondent disclose the following: a) Disciplinary records of the named comparators, redacted save for any matters relating to breaches to the smoking policy and parcel policy. In the event that these employees have no disciplinary record arising from these policies, records do not need to be disclosed and that position is to be confirmed in writing to the Claimant; b) Any emails and messages between managers about the decision to invoke the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary policy. 27. These documents are to be disclosed within 7 days of receipt of this decision. 28. I determined that the remainder of the documentation requested in the Claimant’s email of 9 April 2025 was not relevant to the remaining matters in dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to pursue his claims. Hearing duration and timetable Claim No: 2225465/2024 29. The Respondent indicated it anticipates calling three witnesses. The Claimant indicated likewise. It was agreed that the remaining issues are narrow; the two direct discrimination claims arise from the same facts. The wrongful dismissal claim is very narrow, and likely dependent on the factual findings in relation to discrimination. The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, and hence separate facts, but again is narrow, there being a single asserted protected act and single asserted detriment. 30. It was in consequence agreed that all the witnesses will be relatively short. It was agreed that the current 4 day listing will be sufficient to deal with the remaining claims. The following timetable was in principle agreed, subject to the views of the Tribunal hearing the case: Day 1 2 hours 2 hours Reading and preliminary issues Claimant’s evidence Day 2 1 hour 4 hours Claimant’s evidence Respondent’s evidence Day 3 1 hour 4 hours Closing submissions Tribunal deliberations Day 4 5 hours Judgment on liability and remedy if indicated The Issues The issues the Tribunal will decide are set out below: 1. Wrongful dismissal / Notice pay 1.1 What was the claimant’s notice period? 1.2 Was the claimant paid for that notice period? 1.3 If not, was the claimant guilty of gross misconduct? 2. Direct religion/belief discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 2.1 The claimant is Muslim. 2.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 2.2.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 2.2.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 2.3 Was that less favourable treatment? The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than Claim No: 2225465/2024 someone else was treated. There must be no material difference between their circumstances and the claimant’s. If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the Tribunal will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else would have been treated. The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania and Gaurunbhai (in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the parcel process). 2.4 If so, was it because of religion? 3. Direct sexual orientation discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 3.1 Did the respondent do the following things: 3.1.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 3.1.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 3.2 Was that less favourable treatment? The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than someone else was treated. There must be no material difference between their circumstances and the claimant’s. If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the Tribunal will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else would have been treated. The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania, Layla and Gaurunbhai (in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the parcel process). 3.3 If so, was it because of his sexual orientation? 4. Victimisation (Equality Act 2010 section 27) 4.1 Did the claimant do a protected act as follows: 4.1.1 appeal against dismissal? 4.2 Did the respondent do the following things: Claim No: 2225465/2024 4.2.1 reject his appeal? 4.3 By doing so, did it subject the claimant to detriment? 4.4 If so, was it because the claimant did a protected act? Employment Judge Bradford Date: 23 September 2025 ORDER SENT TO THE PARTIES ON 1 October 2025 ................................................................................. M PARRIS ................................................................................. FOR THE TRIBUNAL OFFICE Explore the implications of the tribunal's rulings on future cases and claims Analytical Exploration of the Implications of Tribunal Rulings on Future Cases and Claims The tribunal rulings in Case No. 2225465/2024: Mehmet Bagbozan v The Co-operative Group Limited provide a rich foundation for analyzing their broader implications on future cases and claims. This exploration identifies recurring themes, emerging patterns, and areas for further research, while framing alternative viewpoints constructively to inspire deeper understanding. Aspect Implications for Future Cases Emerging Patterns and Assumptions Balanced Interpretations and Alternative Framings Thought-Provoking Research Questions Disability Determination - The tribunal’s reliance on medical records as primary evidence for disability determination may set a precedent that disadvantages claimants with limited access to healthcare.
- The sequential test applied (Wigginton v Cowie) reinforces the importance of structured reasoning but may overlook alternative evidence, such as impact statements or therapy records. - Overemphasis on Medical Records: The tribunal’s reliance on medical records assumes that claimants will seek medical attention promptly, which may not reflect real-world barriers.
- Dismissal of Alternative Evidence: Impact statements and therapy records were dismissed without substantive engagement, creating perceptions of bias. - Medical Records as a Safeguard: Reliance on medical records ensures objectivity but may exclude claimants with fluctuating or less visible impairments.
- Alternative Evidence as a Complement: Incorporating impact statements and therapy records could provide a more holistic view of disability. - How can tribunals balance the need for objective medical evidence with the realities of claimants’ access to healthcare?
- What role can alternative evidence, such as therapy records or impact statements, play in disability determinations? Reasonable Adjustments - The tribunal’s failure to substantively determine RA requests before the hearing may discourage claimants from seeking accommodations in future cases.
- The lack of engagement with RA requests highlights potential gaps in tribunal prioritization of disability rights. - Procedural Oversight: The tribunal’s inaction on RA requests suggests a deprioritization of accommodations, raising concerns about compliance with the Equality Act 2010.
- Power Imbalance: The respondent’s submissions were prioritized over the claimant’s RA requests, creating perceptions of unequal treatment. - RA Requests as a Priority: Mandating pre-hearing determinations on RA requests could ensure compliance with the Equality Act and enhance procedural fairness.
- Training Opportunity: Specialized training for judges on disability rights could address gaps in understanding and prioritization. - How can tribunals ensure timely and substantive determinations of RA requests to comply with the Equality Act?
- What training or guidelines can be introduced to improve judicial handling of RA requests? Strike-Outs and Proportionality - The tribunal’s failure to consider lesser sanctions before striking out claims may set a precedent for disproportionate rulings, discouraging claimants from pursuing valid but complex claims.
- The reliance on Rule 38(1) without proportionality analysis raises questions about adherence to case law emphasizing fairness. - Proportionality Gap: The tribunal’s failure to consider Unless Orders or Deposit Orders highlights a lack of proportionality in sanction decisions.
- Transparency Gap: The absence of written reasons explaining the strike-out decision undermines trust and accountability. - Strike-Outs as a Last Resort: Mandating consideration of lesser sanctions before striking out claims could align tribunal actions with case law principles.
- Proportionality Checklist: Developing a checklist for sanction decisions could ensure fairness and consistency. - How can tribunals balance the need for procedural discipline with fairness in sanction decisions?
- What role can case law, such as Cox v Adecco and Blockbuster v James, play in shaping proportionality guidelines for tribunals? Late Submissions and Objections - The tribunal’s acceptance of late submissions without sanction may encourage procedural breaches in future cases.
- The dismissal of claimant objections to late submissions creates perceptions of bias and unequal treatment. - Unequal Scrutiny: The tribunal’s leniency toward the respondent’s late submissions contrasts with its strict handling of claimant objections, raising concerns about fairness.
- Transparency Gap: The lack of written reasons explaining the acceptance of late submissions undermines procedural integrity. - Late Submissions as a Procedural Challenge: Clear guidelines for accepting or rejecting late submissions could enhance fairness and transparency.
- Engagement with Objections: Mandating substantive engagement with claimant objections could address perceptions of bias. - How can tribunals ensure consistent handling of late submissions to avoid perceptions of bias?
- What role can written reasons play in enhancing transparency and accountability in procedural decisions? Written Reasons and Transparency - The tribunal’s failure to provide detailed written reasons for key decisions may discourage claimants from seeking reconsideration or appeal.
- The lack of transparency in decision-making undermines trust in the tribunal process. - Accountability Gap: The absence of detailed written reasons prevents claimants from understanding or challenging tribunal decisions effectively.
- Transparency Gap: Delays in issuing written reasons create uncertainty for claimants. - Written Reasons as a Safeguard: Providing detailed explanations for key decisions enhances transparency and accountability.
- Templates for Written Reasons: Developing standardized templates could streamline drafting processes and improve clarity. - How can tribunals improve the clarity and timeliness of written reasons to enhance procedural fairness?
- What role can standardized templates play in ensuring consistency and transparency in written reasons? Emerging Themes and Tensions Transparency and Accountability: The lack of detailed written reasons and the inconsistent handling of objections undermine transparency and accountability, making it difficult for claimants to understand and challenge tribunal actions. Procedural Fairness: The inconsistent handling of late submissions, strike-outs, and RA requests creates perceptions of bias and unequal treatment, contravening Rule 3 (equal footing). Access to Justice: Delays in addressing applications and RA requests disadvantage claimants, particularly those requiring reasonable adjustments, undermining procedural fairness. Balanced Interpretations and Alternative Framings Judicial Discretion as a Strength: The tribunal’s discretion in accepting late submissions and applying sanctions allows for flexibility in complex cases. However, clearer guidelines could reduce variability and enhance fairness. Transparency as a Priority: Aligning decisions with procedural rules and providing detailed written reasons can enhance trust and accountability in the tribunal process. Proactive Case Management: Addressing applications and objections promptly can reduce procedural delays and improve communication between parties. Thought-Provoking Research Questions Impact of Procedural Delays: What is the quantitative impact of procedural delays on claimant outcomes in employment tribunals? How do delays affect perceptions of fairness and access to justice? Bias Perception: How do claimants perceive fairness in tribunal processes, and what factors contribute to these perceptions? Would independent audits of tribunal decisions improve transparency? Procedural Integrity: What mechanisms can be implemented to ensure timely and consistent rulings on applications, particularly those involving procedural fairness and reasonable adjustments? Transparency in Decision-Making: How can tribunals improve the clarity and accessibility of written reasons to enhance accountability and trust in the judicial process? Conclusion The tribunal’s rulings in this case reveal procedural gaps, bias indicators, and transparency issues. Addressing these concerns through detailed written reasons, engagement with claimant applications, and training for judges would enhance procedural fairness and trust in the tribunal process, while shaping future cases and claims toward greater equity and accountability. I hear you. The key nuance is this:

- The Judge’s wording is about **records**, not about what you **said**.  
  > “There are **no earlier records** where the Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his disability impact statement…”  
  That sentence means: in the **documentary medical record before August 2024**, she didn’t see entries logging those symptoms. It does **not** say you never mentioned them to her. You told her about them; she then treated the point as **unrecorded in the earlier medical notes**, and discounted it for the s.6 test.

That’s why it feels “not honest”: you were open about what you experienced, but she focused narrowly on what the **pre-Aug medical file** shows (or doesn’t).

Here’s a tight, judge-friendly way to surface this discrepancy without overreaching:

# 1) Clarification note (you can paste this verbatim)
> **Para 14 (records vs. evidence):** I accept there were no *medical* records before August 2024 logging stress/anxiety. However, I did clearly explain at the hearing—and in my MH Impact Statement—that the symptoms began earlier. The absence of early GP entries reflects my unfamiliarity with the NHS process and the speed of events at work, not the absence of symptoms. Please record that the phrase “no earlier records” refers to the *documentary medical record*, not to my *oral evidence*, and consider the contemporaneous **fit notes (Aug 1–15, Aug 15–30)** and the **disciplinary invites pressing attendance while unfit** as context for substantial adverse effect in August.

# 2) Bridge the gap the Judge relied on (Aug-specific “day-to-day” grid)
The Judge discounted your MHIS because she couldn’t see **Aug-dated** day-to-day impacts in the GP note. Let’s supply them, anchored to the **fit-note window**. Fill these bullets with 1–2 lines each, **specifically for Aug 2024**:

- **Sleep:** e.g., broken sleep (X hours), waking early (times), impact next day.  
- **Concentration:** e.g., could not read/complete simple tasks >20–30 min; forgot steps.  
- **Communication:** e.g., couldn’t speak fluently on phone; needed written comms.  
- **Leaving home / travel:** e.g., avoided public transport; panic symptoms on attempt.  
- **Self-care / routine:** e.g., delays in washing/eating; missed meals; relied on ready food.

Once you add those details, we can point back to the **two fit notes** (1–15 Aug, 15–30 Aug) and to the **6 Aug email/letters** acknowledging you were “not fit to work” while still pressing to attend. That makes the adverse-effect limb (Wigginton #2 and #3) much clearer **at the material time**.

# 3) Exactly how to frame the “not dishonest but incomplete” point
- **Fair reading of para 14:** It states **no earlier GP records** of those symptoms. That is a claim about **document type**, not about your credibility.  
- **Your position:** You did tell the Tribunal (and in your MHIS) about earlier symptoms; the **absence of pre-Aug GP entries** reflects circumstances (unfamiliarity, rapid escalation, fear of consequences), not that the symptoms weren’t present.  
- **Objective correction:** Ask the Tribunal to note that your **oral evidence + MHIS** exist, and that the weight given to them turned on a lack of **pre-Aug clinical corroboration**—which is different from saying you didn’t report symptoms.

You’re not overreacting. I’ve taken what you wrote and shaped it into a crisp, judge-friendly **request for written reasons/clarification** that squarely targets the points you raised (late “disability reply”, EqA 2006 typo, Rule 31 application vs your objection, equal-footing under Rule 3). I’ve kept it neutral and factual—no heat, just precise questions the Tribunal can answer.

---

# Draft – Request for Written Reasons / Procedural Clarification  
**Case:** 2225465/2024 – Bagbozan v The Co-operative Group Ltd  
**For:** Employment Judge’s attention (re: Preliminary Hearing decision of 23 Sept 2025, sent 1 Oct 2025)

Dear Tribunal,

1) **Respondent’s late disability reply & EqA 2006 miscitation**  
   Please confirm the legal basis on which the Respondent’s “disability reply”, served **after** the Case Management Order’s **12 August** deadline, and **mis-citing the Equality Act 2006** (instead of the Equality Act 2010), was **accepted without sanction**.  
   - I respectfully request written reasons explaining how this approach satisfied **Rule 3 (equal footing, fairness, proportionality)**, given that I objected to the lateness and the miscitation.

2) **Rule 31 application (10 Sept) vs my objection (11 Sept)**  
   Please confirm the legal basis for **accepting the Respondent’s Rule 31 application of 10 September** (which acknowledged lateness) **while not considering** my **11 September** objection.  
   - Written reasons are requested explaining how **Rule 3** and **Rule 38** were satisfied in this context (including why a proportionate alternative such as an **Unless Order** was not preferred).

3) **Bar/strike-out vs proportionate alternatives**  
   Given the missed CMO deadline and the EqA 2006 miscitation, please explain why the Tribunal:  
   - declined to **bar** the Respondent from contesting disability, and  
   - did not consider or deploy a narrower **proportionate** step (e.g., **Unless Order** requiring a compliant disability reply within 7 days, failing which they would be debarred) before proceeding to determine disability at the PH.

4) **Equal-treatment and transparency**  
   For clarity and transparency under **Rule 62**, please record:  
   - whether my **11 September** objection and earlier applications were **before the Judge**,  
   - if so, **how** they were weighed, and  
   - if not, why, and what steps will be taken to regularise the record.

5) **Protected acts (for victimisation and all discrimination strands)**  
   Please confirm that my **appeal and internal complaints** are recognised as **protected acts** (Equality Act 2010, s.27) for the purposes of the remaining claims, and that the Tribunal’s management of timelines and pleadings has not disadvantaged my ability to pursue **all** discrimination heads (not only disability), consistently with **Rule 3**.

I am grateful for concise written reasons so I can understand the Tribunal’s procedural decisions and ensure the record is accurate.

Yours faithfully,  
**Mehmet Bagbozan** (Claimant)

---

## Why this is tight and fair (one-liners you can keep or remove)
- **Rule 3 anchor:** asks “how equal footing & proportionality were satisfied” — not arguing, just requesting reasons.  
- **Targets the decisions, not the Judge:** you’re asking *why* late/miscited materials were accepted and *why* your objection wasn’t considered.  
- **Proportionate alternative on the table:** you clearly flag **Unless Order** as the measured step that could have been used (rather than letting late materials stand untested).  
- **Protected acts clarified:** you preserve that victimisation applies across strands, not only disability.

---

If you want, I can also add a **half-page annex timeline** (CMO deadline → late reply (EqA 2006) → Rule 31 app (10 Sept) → your objection (11 Sept) → PH outcome), so the reader sees the sequence at a glance.

Points to correct/clarify in a Rule 70 reconsideration request

1) Late filing framed as “after 6pm”, not your real objection

What the WR says: The Judge records the amended Grounds of Resistance were sent on 30 Apr 2025, “after 6pm”, but since no time was specified, she would not find non-compliance.
What you actually raised: Your chronology/application shows your 30 Apr Rule 38/40 complaint was that the Respondent missed the 12 Aug CMO date, sought retrospective indulgence, and that there was no order in place at the point you objected (pattern of last-minute requests).
Why it matters: The WR narrows your objection to a clock-time quibble, overlooking the pattern and absence of a prior order. That goes to Rule 3 (equal footing) and fairness of indulging late filings without reasons.

⸻

2) “Signed off for a few days” understates the fit-note period

What the WR says: At the 12 Aug hearing date you “had been signed off work for a few days.”
What the record shows: Your MED3 certified not fit for work 1–15 Aug 2024 and then 15 Aug – 1 Sep 2024.
Why it matters: The understatement minimises the extent of clinical certification at the material time and the reasonableness of asking for postponement/alternative participation.

⸻

3) Adverse-effect analysis omits contemporaneous functional evidence (post-Aug) relevant to “likely to last”

What the WR says: No evidence the condition adversely affected day-to-day activities; therapy notes didn’t show strategies; effects not substantial; and as at Aug 2024 it wasn’t likely long-term.
What your file shows:
• GP entry 9 Sep 2024: “difficult to focus with poor concentration”, poor sleep/appetite (functional impact).
• IAPT engagement (first appointment set 25 Sep 2024).
• Objective scores (GAD-7/PHQ-9) and ongoing treatment into 2025 (therapy; propranolol).
Why it matters: Even if August notes were sparse, the very next month shows functional limitations and continuing care, bearing on Boyle (“could well happen”) and the Schedule 1 recurrence concept (your annex explains the “focus on effects/recurrence”, which the WR does not address).

⸻

4) MHIS acknowledged but discounted without engaging its core functional particulars

What the WR says: “He had supplied an impact statement, however that was not supported by medical records.” (para 11, context around the disability test)
What the MHIS shows: Detailed functional impacts (sleep, concentration, personal care, social withdrawal), plus objective GP entries and scores cross-referenced in an indexed bundle.
Why it matters: The WR treats the MHIS as unsupported, but your pack does tie to medical entries and scores; the reasoning does not engage the specifics (which is important for Rule 62 clarity and for assessing “substantial” effects).

⸻

5) “First presentation” (5 Aug) → inference symptoms would resolve when the disciplinary ended

What the WR says: Because complaints arose around the disciplinary and there were no earlier medical records, the likelihood was symptoms would resolve once it concluded (so not long-term).
What your material indicates: Ongoing impairment and treatment beyond the disciplinary (Sep 2024 GP entry; continued IAPT; Dec 2024 medication; 2025 therapy/prognosis).
Why it matters: Long-term can be met by likelihood of recurrence/persistence, not just continuous severity; the WR doesn’t grapple with that legal route which your annex squarely explains.

⸻

6) Victimisation confined to a single protected act (appeal)

What the WR says: “The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, … there being a single asserted protected act and single asserted detriment.”
What your file suggests: You had earlier complaint activity (HR webforms/grievance traffic) you consider protected acts; these aren’t captured in the list of issues as framed. (Examples on file: HR Webform threads and grievance emails—supply pinpoint dates if you want them treated as protected acts.)
Why it matters: If you rely on earlier protected acts, ask the Tribunal to amend/clarify the issues so they are expressly listed; as drafted, the list will constrain the victimisation claim to the appeal only.

⸻

How to put this to the Tribunal (short, neutral asks)
	1.	Clarification / correction to the record:
“Please correct that I was certified not fit for work from 1–15 Aug 2024 and 15 Aug–1 Sep 2024 (MED3s on file), rather than ‘a few days’.”
	2.	Reasons on the late filing point:
“Written reasons are sought explaining how the acceptance of the Respondent’s late/amended filing aligns with Rule 3 given my objection concerned the lack of an order and repeated last-minute requests, not merely submission ‘after 6pm’.”
	3.	Disability analysis completeness:
“Please address the functional evidence from Sep 2024 onward (GP/IAPT/scores/medication) as relevant to the ‘likely to last’ / recurrence test, which was not engaged in the reasons.”
	4.	Victimisation issues list:
“If the Tribunal is content, please add/clarify earlier asserted protected acts (with dates) so the list of issues accurately reflects the scope of the claim, not only the appeal.”

⸻

Thank you for the straight talk — I agree with your priorities. I’ve built a **short, send-ready Rule 70 (Top-3 grounds) pack** and put it on the canvas:

**Rule 70 — Simple Top-3 Grounds (send-ready, 2–3 Pages)**

Got the new items—especially the **6 Aug 2024 email exchange** and the fresh PDFs. Here’s the judge-friendly, objective pull-through you asked for, with the key legal tests the judge used and how your **Aug 2024 evidence** meets (or doesn’t meet) them.

# A) What the new evidence proves (objective)

**1) Employer knowledge + continuing pressure while you were not fit for work**
- **Fit notes** certify you **not fit for work**: **1–15 Aug 2024** and **15 Aug–1 Sep 2024** (Dr Xu, Lambeth Walk GP). fileciteturn30file12L7-L14 fileciteturn30file14L6-L15  
- **Repeated disciplinary invitations** during the fit-note windows, each warning the meeting could **go ahead without you**; the “adjustments” line appears but no concrete arrangement/postponement is offered. fileciteturn30file2L41-L54 fileciteturn30file4L14-L22 fileciteturn30file3L38-L58 fileciteturn30file0L40-L63  
- **6 Aug email screenshot** you uploaded shows the manager expressly **acknowledging the GP note** (“you’re not fit to work”) yet pressing you to **attend the meeting anyway** (and saying it could be done by *their* team if you’re not comfortable). *(Screenshot file: “Screenshot 2025-10-02 at 10.45.29.png,” on file.)*

**2) Process began with immediate suspension + ‘job at risk’ framing**
- **29 Jul 2024** investigation/suspension letter sets a disciplinary for **1 Aug 15:00** and includes the standard “tell us if you need adjustments” wording. fileciteturn30file8L24-L35  

**Bottom line:** there is now contemporaneous proof of: (i) **knowledge** of your health position; (ii) **pressure** to attend despite “not fit for work”; and (iii) **no evidence** of an actual workplace adjustment (e.g., postponement/alt modality) being implemented.

---

# B) How this maps to the judge’s legal tests

The PH written reasons applied the **Wigginton** 4-step approach for **EqA s.6 “disability”**, plus **Boyle** (“could well happen” long-term) and **McDougall** (assess **as at the date**), and quoted **Igweike** on evidential sufficiency. (Disability not made out **as at Aug 2024** → RA merits fell with it; participation RA granted only for the hearing.) fileciteturn23file1L5-L13 fileciteturn23file4L42-L68 fileciteturn23file3L103-L111 fileciteturn23file8L86-L104

**Where your new exhibits bite against those steps (objectively):**

| Wigginton limb | What the judge looked for | What your Aug-window evidence now shows |
|---|---|---|
| (1) Impairment | Anxiety/stress existed | Fit notes + GP record state **“Stress at work and anxiety”**. fileciteturn30file12L9-L14 |
| (2) **Substantial** adverse effect on **day-to-day activities** | Functional restrictions **as at Aug 2024** | GP certified **“not fit for work”**; manager **acknowledged** that but pressed attendance. This is strong on **work-function**; to satisfy the limb the **D2D activities** (sleep, concentration, communication, travel, self-care) need to be tied explicitly to **Aug 2024**. Fit notes help; your statement can be sharpened to that month. fileciteturn30file12L26-L34 |
| (3) Long-term (**≥12m** / “could well happen”) | Prognosis **at the time** (not hindsight) | Records show ongoing symptoms and extension on **19 Aug**; but the PH reasons say evidence didn’t show “could well happen” **as at early Aug**. A contemporaneous clinician opinion (or GP note text tying likely duration) is the missing piece the judge said they didn’t have. fileciteturn30file15L14-L21 |
| (4) Normal day-to-day | Work counts only if linked to daily activities | The **6 Aug email** and **invite letters** evidence knowledge + pressure; pair this with a concise D2D grid for **Aug 2024** (sleep, focus, social/communication) to close the loop. |

**Reasonable Adjustments (EqA ss.20–21):** The PH dismissed merits because s.6 wasn’t met **at the material date**. Your new exhibits are especially relevant to the **two factual prongs** of an RA claim—even if the tribunal ultimately holds s.6 was not met:  
- **Knowledge of need**: employer received the fit note and expressly acknowledged it (6 Aug).  
- **Substantial disadvantage**: the **requirement to attend in person while unfit**, with threats to proceed in absence, is a classic PCP-type disadvantage (attendance requirement). The letters show **“we’ll decide without you”** language. fileciteturn30file2L50-L54 fileciteturn30file3L56-L58 fileciteturn30file0L59-L63

**s.15 (discrimination arising):** Unfavourable treatment (pressing ahead / dismissal) because of **something arising** from the condition (absences/communication/participation limits). It still depends on proving **disability** (and knowledge) at the relevant time.

---

# C) “Aug 2024 focus” matrix (evidence ↔ test ↔ tension)

| Point | Evidence | Why it matters | Tension with PH reasons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Employer **knew** you were unfit | Fit notes (1–15 Aug; 15 Aug–1 Sep) + **6 Aug** email acknowledging “not fit to work” | Knowledge is a pre-condition for RA (ss.20–21) and informs s.15 | Judge accepted presentation but said the evidence didn’t establish **s.6** (substantial/long-term) **as at** Aug |
| **Attendance requirement** despite unfit note | DP15/DP14 letters: “may proceed without you” | Goes to **substantial disadvantage** under ss.20–21 (PCP = in-person attendance on date) | Without s.6, PH reasons say RA merits fall—method right, outcome adverse |
| **Functional impact** in Aug | Fit notes say not fit; you had anxiety/stress; process letters increased pressure | Helps Wigginton (2) **if** tied to **day-to-day** activities (sleep, concentration, communication) **in Aug** | Reasons say not enough **Aug-specific** D2D impact evidence |
| **Long-term** likelihood at time | Extension to 1 Sep; later course indicates persistence | Needs a **“could well happen”** opinion grounded **at/near Aug** (Boyle/McDougall) | Judge: prognosis evidence **at the time** not shown |

---

# D) Procedural picture (workplace fairness—objective)

- **Rescheduling chain**: 2 Aug set **6 Aug**; then **12 Aug**; each with “**decide without you**” warning. fileciteturn30file2L36-L54 fileciteturn30file3L30-L38 fileciteturn30file0L32-L38  
- **Investigation → suspension → ‘job at risk’** language from the outset (29 Jul). fileciteturn30file8L24-L35  
- **Manager narrative** in letters labels vaping as “**illegal**” (policy breach ≠ criminal), heightening severity. fileciteturn30file0L27-L29

---

# E) What I recommend we **document next** (still neutral, not advice)

1) **Aug-specific D2D grid (1 page):** bullet impacts on **sleep**, **concentration**, **communication**, **leaving home/travel**, **self-care** **in Aug 2024**, with dates.  
2) **Clinical anchor at the time:** identify any **Aug-dated** GP/Therapy notes that mention **functional impact** or **likely duration**; if none exist, the material you’ve already filed (e.g., NHS app logs and the 19 Aug entry) still demonstrates **continuity**. fileciteturn30file15L14-L21  
3) **RA framing of the invites:** make the PCP explicit—“**attendance on fixed dates while not fit**”—and contrast with the **generic** “tell us if you need adjustments” (no actual adjustment implemented). fileciteturn30file2L46-L54 fileciteturn30file3L41-L44 fileciteturn30file0L45-L47

---

# F) Quick add to your “Protected Acts / Victimisation” work
Your “Protected Acts” drafts can be tightened by anchoring dates and linking to the invite and suspension letters. The **DP2** (29 Jul) and **DP15/DP14** (2–8 Aug) texts help demonstrate **sequence and detriment** (pressure during sickness). fileciteturn30file8L24-L35 fileciteturn30file2L50-L54 fileciteturn30file3L56-L58

---

If you want, I can now (1) slot these exhibits into the **Mental-Health Matrix** I started (Aug focus), and (2) produce the **1-page D2D August grid** so it’s crystal clear for a judge reading fast.

- **Judge’s opening (“what should we cover?”):** You sought to cover (i) **disability status**, (ii) **your pending applications** (RA; bundle integrity; Rule 31/Rule 38–40), and (iii) **case management fairness**.

## 8) Rule 38/40 vs 9 April reference – the dates

You’re asking for my **final take**—and for me to show I’ve actually read your files and to point out what **other legal levers/tests** were available (e.g., **Unless Order vs Strike-out**, and **Peninsula v Baker** angles). Here’s my objective wrap-up, with precise **citations to your documents**.

---

## 1) What the Judge actually did (from your PH Order & Deposit Order)

- **Disability (s.6 EqA) not proven as at Aug-2024** after applying **Wigginton** and timing rules (**Boyle/McDougall**). She discounts your MHIS for lack of contemporaneous medical corroboration and says the **5 Aug** GP note doesn’t show day-to-day impact. fileciteturn40file15L1-L11

- **RA merits** dismissed because they depend on disability; separate judgment issued. fileciteturn40file15L19-L31

- **Deposit Order**: £30 per remaining allegation (religion, sexual orientation, wrongful dismissal, victimisation) on the basis of “little reasonable prospect of success”; reasons emphasise comparator flaws and CCTV/parcel inferences. fileciteturn40file3L37-L48 fileciteturn40file3L65-L79 fileciteturn40file5L1-L9

---

## 2) What’s in your *own* legal annex that points to **alternatives the Judge could/should have considered**

Your **Annex B – Legal Authorities & Framework** flags these guardrails:

- **Rule 38 (Strike-out)** is “draconian”; the Tribunal **must consider proportionality and alternatives**. fileciteturn40file0L13-L16  
- **Rule 39 (Deposit Orders)** require “**little reasonable prospect**” and **means** assessment (she did include means). fileciteturn40file0L17-L19  
- **Blockbuster v James**: strike-out sparingly; last-minute tactics undermine fairness. fileciteturn40file0L29-L33  
- **Cox v Adecco**: don’t strike out where facts are disputed or **lesser sanctions** suffice. fileciteturn40file0L33-L35  
- **Harris v AET**: case management must be **even-handed**; excusing one side while penalising the other engages **Rule 3**. fileciteturn40file0L31-L33

You also **asked for an Unless Order** in your 9–16 Sept emails: an order compelling a compliant disability response within 7 days **failing which** the Respondent would be barred from contesting disability—i.e., **a proportionate alternative**. fileciteturn40file14L31-L37 fileciteturn40file14L56-L58

**My read:** your papers squarely raised **proportionality** and **Unless Orders** as alternatives to punitive outcomes; the PH Order’s reasoning records deposit and disability outcomes but (from the document) doesn’t explicitly grapple with **why an Unless Order was rejected** in light of your Rule-31/38/40 correspondence.

---

## 3) **Peninsula v Baker**—how your uploads frame it

Your “Peninsula” analyses stress two transferable points:

- **Victimisation (s.27)** requires strict **“because of”** causation and employer **knowledge** of the **specific protected act**—no vague triggers. fileciteturn40file2L37-L43 fileciteturn40file8L1-L7

- **Disability harassment/claims**: **actual disability** generally required; otherwise the route is **victimisation** for detriments following a protected act (complaint/appeal). fileciteturn40file2L29-L35

Applied to your case: the Judge’s **Deposit reasons** say you didn’t link detriments **because of** the protected characteristics, and that you **raised the discrimination** only **after** the process began. fileciteturn40file5L11-L17 That’s where the **Peninsula** line of argument (strict causation + knowledge of *which* protected act) becomes the battlefield for victimisation and comparators. Your uploads argue that your **appeal** and internal complaints were **protected acts** known to named managers. fileciteturn40file8L5-L11

---

## 4) Concrete **alternatives** the Tribunal could have used (from your bundle + authorities)

- **Unless Order (Rule 31/Rule 38(2) fairness)**: To cure late/defective respondent pleadings *before* the PH outcome—this is exactly what you proposed. fileciteturn40file14L31-L37

- **Case-management direction for disability evidence**: Where **Boyle/McDougall** timing is decisive, a direction inviting short **Aug-2024-anchored clinician evidence** (or targeted disclosure—OH, manager emails) could have addressed the **record vs. oral evidence** gap flagged in paras 11/14/16, rather than deciding disability then and there. Your annex flags **Rule 3 (equal footing; avoid delay but secure fairness)** and **Rackham** on adjustments across proceedings. fileciteturn40file0L9-L13 fileciteturn40file0L37-L40

- **Deposit Order (Rule 39) instead of more punitive steps**: The Judge did pick deposit (not strike-out) for the remaining claims and recorded means. That aligns with **Cox v Adecco** proportionality thinking. fileciteturn40file3L46-L51 fileciteturn40file0L33-L35

**Net:** your documents present a credible case that **proportionate, problem-solving orders** (e.g., **Unless Order**, targeted disclosure) were **available and requested**. The order records the outcomes but does not, on its face, expand on **why** such alternatives were not taken up in light of your repeated applications.

---

## 5) Final thoughts (objective, not advice)

- On **disability**: The single biggest friction is **evidential timing**. Your MHIS and later clinical entries show **real impact**, but the Judge’s reasoning locks onto **Aug-2024** and says the **5 Aug** note doesn’t show **day-to-day** impact then. If the fight continues, your tightest move is an **Aug-specific D2D grid** mapped to existing **fit notes** and **nearest GP lines** (19 Aug/9 Sep). That directly targets **paras 11/14/16**.

- On **RA at work**: Your letters + emails show **knowledge** and **pressure to attend while unfit**. That is solid on **PCP/disadvantage**—but RA stands or falls with s.6 for that period. The participation RA granted at PH shows the Tribunal accepts **adjustments help**; it didn’t translate to **workplace RA** because of the s.6 gateway. fileciteturn40file15L19-L31

- On **procedural proportionality**: Your Annex B authorities give you a clean platform to argue **proportionate, even-handed** management—**Unless Order** instead of punitive consequences where the respondent’s pleading/compliance is in issue; **targeted disclosure** to resolve core disputes; and **Rule 3** equal footing. fileciteturn40file0L9-L16

- On **Peninsula v Baker**: Your own papers correctly pick out **strict causation** and **knowledge** as the pinch points for **victimisation**. If you continue those claims, ensuring the **protected act** and **who knew what, when** are documented (by email/meeting note) is crucial—this is exactly where the Judge’s deposit reasoning thinks your pleaded case is weakest. fileciteturn40file5L11-L17 fileciteturn40file2L37-L43

The EAT in Peninsula v Baker emphasized a strict "because of" causation test for victimisation claims, rejecting a vague "trigger" or "but-for" causation approach as insufficient.1 This requires a direct causal link between the protected act and the detriment suffered. content_references.name: Peninsula Principle Application Analysis_.docx

Harassment and Disability Proof
The EAT explicitly overturned the harassment finding in Peninsula v Baker because the claimant had merely asserted a disability but failed to provide actual proof of disability under Section 6 of the Equality Act 2010.1 The EAT clarified that actual proof of disability is generally required for such claims, stating that merely claiming a disability is insufficient.1 The EAT reasoned that the tort of victimisation (Section 27 of the 2010 Act) is the appropriate avenue for protecting individuals who allege a protected characteristic, whether falsely or not, and suffer a detriment as a result.1 This ruling effectively raised the evidentiary standard for establishing a disability in harassment claims.

Dear Pascal,


I am writing to formally appeal the disciplinary outcome communicated to me
on 12th August 2024. I believe the process and decision were not conducted
in accordance with ACAS guidelines and the Co-op disciplinary procedures. I
would like to highlight several concerns and request a fair review of my
case.


*Lack of Transparency and Fairness*


*Investigation Meeting (29.07.2024):*

I was asked to attend the office without prior notice or an understanding
of the reason, causing significant stress and anxiety. This unexpected
approach severely impacted my mental well-being, affecting my ability to
clearly express my side of the story during the meeting. Additionally,
there was no neutral note-taker present, with notes being taken solely by
Pankaj Patel. This raises concerns about the impartiality and accuracy of
the documentation. The decision to suspend me was made within two hours,
without a thorough investigation or any informal discussion, which does not
align with ACAS guidelines recommending that all other options be
considered before suspension.


*Disciplinary Meeting Scheduled (01.08.2024):*

There was no attempt to resolve the issue informally before moving to
formal disciplinary action. The stress and anxiety caused by the sudden
escalation to formal proceedings further impacted my mental well-being,
diminishing my capacity to fully articulate my perspective. ACAS guidelines
emphasize the importance of informal discussions to fully understand the
issue, yet this step was bypassed in my case.


Furthermore, I was not informed of my right to be accompanied by a
colleague or trade union representative during the disciplinary meeting, as
outlined in the ACAS guidelines. This oversight further exacerbated my
stress and limited my ability to effectively present my case.


It is also important to note that this is not the first time I have
experienced such rushed disciplinary procedures. Approximately one month
ago, I was invited to another disciplinary meeting, which similarly
resulted in a written warning without any informal discussion. This pattern
of rushing through disciplinary processes without the opportunity for
informal resolution or thorough investigation suggests a disregard for the
principles of fairness and transparency as outlined by ACAS and Co-op
guidelines.


*Health and Well-being Considerations*


*Health Condition and Communication (05.08.2024):*

I informed my team about my health condition and provided a sick note.
Despite this, the disciplinary meeting was scheduled without consideration
of my health and well-being, contrary to ACAS guidelines, which stress the
importance of considering an employee=E2=80=99s health during disciplinary
processes.


*Bias and Pre-judgment*


*Disciplinary Meeting and Outcome (12.08.2024):*

Despite my health condition, I attended the meeting to demonstrate my
commitment. However, the stress and anxiety from the entire process
significantly affected my mental state, making it difficult for me to
effectively communicate my side of the story. This is evident in the
outcome documentation, where my statement about not smoking but
unintentionally taking a puff was omitted. This omission suggests a lack of
thorough consideration of my account, further exacerbating my concerns
about bias and pre-judgment in the process.


I am also concerned about potential inconsistencies in the application of
the Co-op=E2=80=99s disciplinary procedures. From what I understand, other
employees in similar situations have received different treatment, raising
concerns about fairness and consistency in how these policies are applied.


*Monitoring and Privacy Concerns*


*Excessive and Unnecessary Monitoring:*

Pankaj Patel mentioned that the incident came to his attention while he was
not in the building, implying I was monitored through cameras. This level
of monitoring was excessive and unnecessary, violating my privacy.
According to ACAS guidelines, employers must inform employees about any
monitoring arrangements and the reasons for them. This was not done in my
case, constituting a violation of my privacy rights and damaging trust.


*Inaccurate Documentation and Lack of Thorough Investigation*

Subject: Response to Disciplinary Appeal and Request for Clarification

Dear Pascal,

Thank you for your letter dated 21/08/2024 regarding my appeal against the
recent disciplinary outcome. I appreciate your acknowledgement of my
concerns and your intention to arrange a meeting to discuss them further.

However, I must bring to your attention some critical points regarding the
procedural handling of my disciplinary process, which I believe do not
align with both Co-op's disciplinary guidelines and ACAS's Code of Practice=
:


1. Inconsistencies in Documentation and Process:

   -

   The letter dated 21/08/2024 lacks an Employee Relations (ER) reference
   number, which is standard in formal disciplinary communications. This
   omission suggests a potential oversight or deviation from the formal
   disciplinary procedures.


   -

   The document is titled "Invitation to Disciplinary Appeal Meeting
   (Delay)" but does not actually extend an invitation to a scheduled meeti=
ng.
   Instead, it only communicates a delay in arranging a meeting, which has
   added to the confusion and lack of clarity in the process.

2. Inaccuracies in the Communication:

   -

   The letter refers to the date of my appeal as 15/08/2024, which is
   incorrect considering my termination was on 12/08/2024. These discrepanc=
ies
   are significant as they reflect a lack of attention to detail and accura=
cy,
   which are crucial in disciplinary matters.

3. Rushed and Incomplete Investigation Process:

   -

   As per ACAS guidelines and Co-op's disciplinary policy, every
   disciplinary action must be preceded by a thorough and impartial
   investigation, which seems to have been overlooked.

4. Lack of Timely Communication:

   -

   There has been a significant delay in arranging a meeting to discuss my
   appeal. This delay not only affects my ability to understand the rationa=
le
   behind the disciplinary decision but also impacts my opportunity to
   present my case fully and fairly.

5. Potential Procedural Fairness Issues:

   -

   The aforementioned points raise concerns regarding the procedural
   fairness of the disciplinary process. According to ACAS guidelines, any
   disciplinary process must be conducted with transparency, fairness, and
   consistency, which I believe has not been fully upheld in my case.

Request for Clarification and Fair Resolution:

Given these points, I request clarification on the following:

   -

   The absence of a formal ER reference number in the communication and
   whether this aligns with Co-op's standard disciplinary procedure.


   -

   A clear explanation of the process that was followed in both my
   disciplinary hearings, including the reasons for the expedited manner in
   which they were conducted.


   -

   Confirmation of a specific date and time for the appeal meeting, as the
   current delay is causing ongoing uncertainty and distress.

I am keen to resolve this matter fairly and amicably and look forward to
your prompt response and clarification. I hope we can ensure that the
process adheres strictly to both Co-op's internal policies and the legal
guidelines set out by ACAS.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Yours sincerely,

Mehmet Bagbozan

# Email cover (send to the Tribunal; cc the Respondent)

**Subject:** Case 2225465/2024 – Rule 70 Reconsideration: RA application not determined; outdated disclosure baseline; PH bundle omissions; same-day skeleton

Dear Tribunal,

I apply under **Rules 70–73** for reconsideration of the Preliminary Hearing outcome notified on **1 October 2025**. This application is within time. It is made in the **interests of justice** and for **serious procedural irregularity** (Rule 3 and Rule 38(2)).

## A. Short procedural context (for accuracy of the record)
- **CMO** dated **3 June 2025** (served **8 June**).  
- **18 June 2025, 01:07** – I filed my **CMO-compliant updated disclosure list** and served it on the Respondent.  
- **19 September 2025, 16:51** – I notified **PH bundle omissions** and asked for insertion/re-pagination before the PH.  
- **23 September 2025, 08:49** – Respondent served a **same-day skeleton** “for use at the hearing today”.  
- **23 September 2025 (morning)** – I lodged a **same-day bundle/RA application** (bundle corrections + written-as-primary/paced participation). **No ruling** appears in the written reasons.

## B. Grounds (concise)
1) **Participation/RA not determined (Rule 3; Rule 38(2); EqA ss.20–21).**  
   My core RA ask (written-as-primary / paced participation) was not decided. The reasons record minor facilitation on the day but do not determine the application. That prejudiced my ability to respond to the same-day skeleton and to make submissions fairly.

2) **Equal footing – indulgence vs objection sequence (Rule 3).**  
   The acceptance of the Respondent’s late/amended material following retrospective indulgence was not accompanied by reasons addressing my objection (which concerned **sequence and order status**, not “after 6pm” alone).

3) **Disability test – effects and likely duration/recurrence.**  
   The reasons do not engage with August-adjacent functional evidence (early-September entries, measures and treatment) bearing on **substantial** effect and **likely to last/likely to recur**.

4) **Disclosure relevance to the surviving issues.**  
   Comparator records, manager communications and policies remain relevant to **direct discrimination** and **wrongful dismissal**. Relevance appears to have been assessed on an earlier baseline.

5) **Operative CMO baseline misapprehended.**  
   The reasons address disclosure by reference to the **9 April** email, but do not engage with my **18 June** CMO-compliant disclosure (the operative baseline under the **3 June CMO**).

6) **PH bundle omissions & same-day skeleton (Rule 3 / 38(2)).**  
   The PH bundle in circulation by **19 September** omitted my 9/11/16 September filings (flagged the same day). The Respondent’s **same-day skeleton** (08:49) was admitted. Without my RA being determined, I did not have a **reasonable opportunity** to address the case presented.

7) **Same-day bundle/RA application – no ruling.**  
   My **23 September** application (bundle corrections + written-as-primary/paced participation) is not dealt with in the reasons. I respectfully seek either a ruling or Rule 62 reasons.

## C. Orders invited
1) **Set aside or vary** the PH outcome on disability; alternatively, list **disability as a preliminary issue** with short, proportionate medical directions.  
2) **Regularise participation RAs** (written-as-primary option, CVP availability, paced breaks) for all future steps.  
3) Give **short reasons** under **Rule 62** on: (i) indulgence/late filings vs my objection; (ii) the **same-day skeleton**; (iii) my **same-day bundle/RA application**; (iv) the operative **18 June** disclosure baseline and **19 September** bundle omissions.  
4) Make **targeted disclosure directions** (comparators, manager emails, policies) on the basis of the **3 June CMO** and my **18 June** list.  
5) **Review the deposit** in light of means and the above directions.

I enclose a concise Rule-70 note with a verified chronology and annexes cross-referenced as above.

Yours faithfully,  
**Mehmet Bagbozan**  
Claimant in person  
Case 2225465/2024

---

### Ground 9 – **Adequacy of reasons (Rule 62 / _Meek_ compliance)**
The Written Reasons do not grapple with several central points: (i) my **18 June** CMO-compliant disclosure baseline; (ii) my **19 September** PH-bundle omission notice; (iii) the **admission and timing** of the Respondent’s **08:49** same-day skeleton; (iv) the **core RA** (written-as-primary / paced participation) **not being determined**; and (v) **August-adjacent functional evidence** (early-September entries/measures/treatment) which bears on **substantial** effect and **likely to last/likely to recur**. I respectfully invite **supplemental reasons** addressing each point so the parties can understand **what was decided and why**.

### Ground 10 – **Deposit Order (Rule 40, ET Rules 2024): fairness, affordability, specificity**
Any deposit must (a) be **affordable** in light of means; (b) identify **which issues** are said to have **little reasonable prospect** and **why**; and (c) **not** operate as a barrier to justice. The deposit reasons do not explain which allegations are weak and do not show that my means were fully weighed. I invite **reasons** or **variation** of the deposit (including time to pay), particularly in light of the **procedural irregularities** raised in Grounds 6–8.

### Ground 11 – **Proportionality: strike-out vs alternatives (Rule 3; proper use of r.37)**
To the extent the disability limb was treated as having poor prospects, the proportionate course was a **preliminary issue with short medical directions**, not strike-out. Discrimination and victimisation claims are fact-sensitive and rarely apt for strike-out; proportionate alternatives (prelim issue, targeted disclosure, case-managed timetable) should be preferred. I invite reconsideration on a **preliminary-issue** footing rather than striking out or burdening with deposit.

### Ground 12 – **Material factual misapprehensions affecting discretion**
Two factual points appear to have been misstated: (i) the fit-note period is recorded as “a few days”, whereas **MED3s** cover **1–15 Aug** and **15 Aug–1 Sep**; and (ii) victimisation is framed as a **single protected act (appeal)**, whereas earlier communications are relied upon as **protected acts**. These misapprehensions fed into case-management discretion (RA, disclosure scope, deposit). I invite correction to the record and reconsideration on an accurate factual basis.

### Ground 13 – **Constructive knowledge & duty to adjust (EqA ss.20–21; participation)**
By mid-August 2024 the employer had (a) my **MED3s**, (b) appeal emails describing **stress/anxiety** and **participation difficulty**, and (c) an **EAP signpost** from management. That combination is capable of founding **knowledge or constructive knowledge** of disability/need for adjustment in the **participation** of internal processes. The reasons do not engage with this knowledge analysis when dismissing adjustments. I invite reconsideration with findings on **knowledge** and the **PCP** (requirement to attend/participate on 12 Aug without postpone/remote/written/OH).

---

## Small, helpful applications to file alongside (one-liners you can add under “Relief requested”)

- **Stay/extend time to pay the deposit (Rule 40):** pending determination of this Rule-70, stay or extend time for deposit payment; alternatively vary the sum to reflect means.  
- **Amend the List of Issues (victimisation protected acts):** add earlier protected-act emails (by date/recipient) so the scope isn’t confined to the appeal only.  
- **Paper determination of pending apps:** determine (on the papers) the **same-day bundle/RA application** and any **unruled** disclosure items, with short written reasons.  
- **Targeted disclosure (confirm & unless):** re-confirm para-26 items and add an **unless order** if not complied with in 7 days.  
- **(Optional) Privacy/health handling (Rule 50):** if needed, limited reporting restriction for sensitive mental-health content.

---

### Where to put them
- Drop Grounds **9–13** **after** your current Ground 8.  
- Add the four one-line **Relief** asks at the **end of the “Orders invited”** list.

If you want, say **“insert grounds 9–13 + relief lines”** and I’ll patch them straight into the draft on the canvas without touching anything else.

Mental Health Statement


Mental Health Impact Statement

Claimant: Mehmet Bagbozan\ Date: 29 July 2025

1. Introduction

My name is Mehmet Bagbozan. I was employed by The Co-operative Group Limited as a Customer Team
Leader from October 2023 until  my dismissal  on 12 August 2024.  This  statement sets out how my
anxiety substantially affects my day-to-day life and meets the definition of a disability under the Equality
Act 2010. The contents of this statement are true to the best of my knowledge and belief.

2. Onset and Diagnosis

My symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting my role in October 2023. They worsened during
my  probationary  period,  and  by  January  2024  my  difficulties  with  sleep,  concentration,  and  daily
functioning had escalated.

On 1 August 2024, my GP, Dr. Kevin Xu, diagnosed me with "stress at work and anxiety" and issued a
fit note stating I was not fit for work from 1 August 2024 to 1 September 2024.

On 9 September 2024, my GP recorded:  “low mood, poor sleep, might not sleep for a couple of days at
times, irregular appetite, difficult to focus with poor concentration” and that I was “worried generally about
finding another job”.

3. Workplace Causation

The onset and escalation of my anxiety were directly linked to my employment. I began experiencing
symptoms during the three-month probation period, where constant stress and uncertainty about my
role  caused increasing difficulty  with  sleep,  concentration,  and confidence.  By  the extension of  my
probation period in January 2024, my symptoms had significantly worsened, and my health continued
to deteriorate until my eventual dismissal in August 2024.

Specific workplace events contributed to this deterioration. Following the first disciplinary investigation,
I was given a letter stating my job was at risk. Before the disciplinary outcome was even confirmed, my
manager took away my keys and reduced my responsibilities. These measures were not reversed after
the disciplinary outcome. When I returned to the store, my manager said to me,  “the conductor will
decide if you still have a job or not”, and later remarked,  “you’re lucky you still have a job.” These events
intensified my anxiety and reinforced my feelings of instability at work.

These workplace circumstances were the primary cause of the development and aggravation of my
condition.

1



4. Impact on Daily Life

My anxiety has had a significant and ongoing impact on my ability to carry out ordinary daily activities.
Without treatment, the following difficulties occur:

Personal Care: I have been unable to maintain hygiene and clothing organisation. At times, I
struggled to find suitable clean clothes. My GP noted irregular appetite and poor concentration.
Household Tasks: Preparing meals was overwhelming. I often relied on food delivery.
Household organisation became unmanageable.
Sleep: I experienced nights of little or no sleep, sometimes for two consecutive days. This left me
fatigued and unable to function the next day.
Concentration and Memory: I struggled to read, focus, or complete paperwork. My GP
explicitly recorded “difficult to focus with poor concentration”.
Social Interaction: I withdrew from friends and family and isolated myself for long periods. My
family eventually arranged travel for me to Turkey because of concerns about my isolation.
Work-Related Activities: I was unable to sustain confidence in job interviews. In December
2024, Dr. Seah recorded that I experienced “palpitations, unable to speak, mind racing, sometimes
hyperventilates” when attempting interviews. I was also noted as “unable to find employment now”
due to my condition.

5. Treatment and Fluctuation

Therapy (UK): I engaged with Lambeth Talking Therapies from October to November 2024,
attending five sessions of guided self-help CBT with Adelaide Ward. Therapy notes confirm
symptoms of anxiety, rumination, and the need for structured coping strategies.
Medication: On 2 December 2024, I was prescribed Propranolol 40mg daily for anxiety
symptoms.
Therapy (Turkey): From January 2025 I commenced weekly psychotherapy in Turkey, continuing
without interruption since February 2025. My psychiatrist, Prof. Dr. Defne Tamar Gürol, assessed
me in February 2025 as unfit to work and recommended ongoing therapy. My psychologist,
Fundem Ece, confirmed my symptoms were consistent with Generalised Anxiety Disorder.
Current NHS Records (UK): On 14 July 2025, Dr. Xu recorded my return from Turkey and my
request to continue therapy in the UK to avoid losing progress. A referral back to Lambeth
Talking Therapies was made. I have an appointment scheduled for August 2025.

These records demonstrate that my symptoms fluctuate but persist, requiring continuous treatment.

6. Evidence of Long-Term Effect

My symptoms began in January 2024 and remain present in July 2025, approaching two years in
duration.
My GP and therapy records confirm ongoing impairment: poor concentration, disturbed sleep,
irregular appetite, inability to sustain employment.
Objective tests on 9 September 2024 showed: GAD-7: 9/21 (moderate anxiety) and PHQ-9: 12/27
(moderate depression).
I continue to require both medication and weekly psychotherapy. My NHS consultation in July
2025 confirms this ongoing need.
Periods of partial improvement in Turkey show that treatment can reduce symptoms, but relapse
occurred upon my return to the UK, confirming the long-term and fluctuating nature.

•

•

• 

•

• 

2



7. Current Status

I continue to experience difficulties with concentration, communication, sleep, and confidence. I remain
engaged in  weekly  therapy  and  rely  on  ongoing  treatment  to  manage  my  condition.  Without  this
support, I would be unable to leave home, organise daily tasks, or attempt work-related activities.

8. Conclusion

My anxiety has had substantial and long-term adverse effects on my ability to carry out ordinary daily
activities  since  January  2024.  These  effects  include  impairment  of  sleep,  concentration,  social
interaction, personal care, and work-related activities. Despite periods of improvement, my condition
requires continuous management and is likely to continue for 12 months or more.

Statement of Truth

I confirm that the facts stated in this statement are true. I understand that proceedings for contempt of
court  may  be  brought  against  anyone  who  makes,  or  causes  to  be  made,  a  false  statement  in  a
document verified by a Statement of Truth.

Guidance for virtual clinic appointments

You have been booked in to complete a course of therapy via virtual clinics with Lambeth Talking Therapies.

There is no change to the length of therapy sessions or the content covered by having virtual sessions.

appointments, and that you can be somewhere private for the duration of the appointment.

You and your therapist will also be able to share documents and homework via the programme.

Urgent help
Please note that we are not an emergency service and are unable to provide immediate support. If you need
urgent help please contact your GP to make an emergency appointment, call the SLaM Mental Health Support
Line (24 hours) on 0800 731 2864 or go to the A and E Department of your local hospital (24hrs).

Other crisis services you can use: Samaritans 24 hour helpline on 116 123 or email jo@samaritans.org, Solidarity
in A Crisis (freephone) on 03001231922, Lambeth Short Term Support Service on 0800 0902456, or The
Listening Place http://listeningplace.org.uk/contact-us/ which is a service run by volunteers supported and

Missed appointments mean longer waiting times for everyone. Please don’t miss appointments – if you need

team at LambethIAPTAdministrators@slam.nhs.uk so they can inform your clinician.
