not call us beforehand to cancel, you may lose that session. Furthermore, if you are late for your session we might
not be able to see you, and this would also count as a missed appointment.  

Treatment sessions not cancelled and not attended without warning

If you do not attend without giving notice, this session might be deducted from the total number of sessions that
will be offered to you.

If you do not attend your session, you will need to contact us within 48 hours of the missed appointment in order
to ensure that your next appointment will take place. If you contact us after this 48hour period then we may still
be able to rebook you, but we will be unable to guarantee you the same appointment time and you may have to
wait. 

If you have to cancel two appointments, you will be discharged and treatment will end. If there are major
unavoidable reasons that stop you coming, please let us know and you may then be able to restart treatment at a
later date when you know you are able to commit to regular attendances. 

Appointments cancelled by us 
We will try hard to offer you good treatment on a regular basis at a convenient time. However sometimes we will
need to alter or cancel an appointment (for example, due to illness). If your therapist needs to cancel an
appointment we will give you as much notice as possible. We will reschedule any sessions cancelled by us: they
will NOT be deducted from the time available for your treatment or reduce the number of sessions available. 

Timekeeping 
It is important that you arrive at your sessions on time. If you are late for a session, you may not be seen. The
session will not be allowed to extend beyond the allotted time frame, therefore any lateness will result in a shorter
session. 

Confidentiality
The information you give is confidential within the NHS. That means it is not disclosed outside of the NHS
unless we have your permission. However, we will inform other people if we think you are at risk to yourself or
to other people. For example if we were concerned that you may be about to harm yourself or another adult or
child. Then we would be required to inform other authorities.

Questionnaires
Your therapist will ask you to complete questionnaires about how you are feeling and doing, every week. This is



essential so that we can keep track of your progress. They will also ask you to do other tasks in your week,
including completing diaries for homework. This is to make sure that what we do works in your everyday life.

Research opportunity
If you are interested in taking part in research, Lambeth Talking Therapies is collaborating with the Genetic
Links to Anxiety and Depression (GLAD) Study. This would allow you to take part in research studies about
psychological wellbeing and talking therapies. The goal is to better understand anxiety and depression and to
improve treatment for anyone who has experienced these difficulties. For more information, see the attached
leaflet or visit www.gladstudy.org.uk.

http://www.gladstudy.org.uk/


 
What is Guided Self-Help?

Guided self-help is a form of therapy involving self-help materials based on Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy (CBT). 
You will be supported by a Psychological Wellbeing Practitioner to learn techniques to help manage symptoms of 
depression, anxiety, panic attacks, phobias and stress. You will be asked to do some in-between session tasks and the
emphasis will be on providing you with techniques and coping strategies that you can use independently in the long
term. 

What happens in Guided Self-Help sessions?

The sessions are offered weekly, typically up to 6 sessions.  Each treatment session will last up to 30 minutes;
therefore sessions will be focused and structured in order for you to get the most out of your treatment. Guided
self-help is a collaborative treatment, so together in each session, you and a Psychological Wellbeing Practitioner will
aim to:

l Set an agenda for the session
l Identify your priorities and goals for the session
l Work through a range of guided self-help booklets
l Guide you in how to use the guided self-help techniques and apply them to your daily life
l Set in-between session tasks to help you practice the techniques
l Review how you get on with in-between session tasks

What are in-between session tasks and why are they important?

In-between session (or ‘homework’) tasks are set at the end of each session and are a key method of change in guided
self-help. As the sessions are only 30 minutes long, most of the practical work will be done outside of sessions. This
enables you to try out the techniques in your everyday life and test out how well they work for you.

It is important to complete the in-between session tasks because many of the techniques will be new and will need to
be developed through repeated practice. Regular practice of the techniques is essential in order for change to come
about and for you to see improvements in symptoms of depression and anxiety.

How is Guided self-help delivered?

Guided self-help can be done individually or with a group of people. It can also be done using self-help materials or
an online computer programme.  It can be delivered in person, over the phone or virtually.

How effective is Guided self-help?

Guided self-help is the first-line intervention recommended by the NICE guidelines for a range of anxiety disorders
and depression.  It is most effective when sessions are attended regularly and when in-between sessions tasks are
completed.

Good Thinking

Good Thinking is a digital wellbeing site that includes information, advice, quizzes, self-assessments and links to
helpful apps and tools to help manage a variety of different conditions such as sleep issues, stress, anxiety and low
mood. Their website provides a variety of interesting, helpful and free podcasts, videos, webinars and blogs that aim
to promote positive mental wellbeing. This is an excellent resource to use while you wait for treatment, during
treatment, or to even keep learning CBT skills after treatment has finished to aid recovery.

ACE ACTIVITY 

Aim for a healthy life balance:  Achieve, Connect, Enjoy 

Our mood can be greatly affected by what we do, when, and with whom.  

In order to maintain a healthy sense of wellbeing, we need 
to balance what we do.  We can use the acronym ACE to 

help us remember: 

 ACHIEVE - work, chores, study 

 CONNECT -  with friends, family, community 

 ENJOY – play, fun, pleasure 

When we feel stressed, we often spend more time doing 

things that help us achieve, but less of enjoyment and 

connecting with others.   When we feel depressed, we 

withdraw and isolate ourselves and do much less, and 

when we feel anxious, we tend to avoid places or people 

where we feel anxious. 

Make time for yourself each day - relaxation, fun, enjoyment. Create a healthy balance 

- allow time for activities which give you a sense of achievement, those that give a 

sense of connecting with and of being close to others, and of a sense of enjoyment.  

These activities affect our brain chemistry by acting directly on the release of neuro-

transmitters, and are our natural anti-stress and anti-depressants. 

 Achievement stimulates dopamine 
 Purposeful activity stimulates serotonin 

 Connecting with other people stimulates oxytocin  

 Exercise stimulates endorphins 

Therefore, making sure we keep doing these ACE activities every day, will help us 

overcome our problems. 

 Keep an ACE Log to help you keep track   (www.get.gg/docs/ACELog.pdf) 
 Or use the weekly planner                       (www.get.gg/docs/WeeklyPlanner.pdf) 

The BACE acronym includes looking after your body: 

 BODY CARE - exercise, healthy eating and drinking, rest 

 ACHIEVE - work, chores and study 

 CONNECT WITH OTHERS - friends, family and community 

 ENJOY - play, fun, pleasure

Here’s a **full, ready-to-send** Rule 70 reconsideration email you can copy/paste as-is. I’ve kept it tight, judge-friendly, and focused on the **four strongest grounds**.

---

**Subject:** Case 2225465/2024 — Rule 70 Reconsideration: RA not determined; outdated disclosure baseline; PH bundle omissions; same-day skeleton

**To:** London Central Employment Tribunal  
**Cc:** Respondent (Peninsula)  
**Case:** 2225465/2024 – Mehmet Bagbozan v The Co-operative Group Ltd

Dear Tribunal,

I apply under **Rules 70–73** for reconsideration of the Preliminary Hearing outcome **sent on 1 October 2025**. This application is in time and is made in the **interests of justice** for **serious procedural irregularity** (including breaches of **Rule 3** and **Rule 38(2)**).

## A. Short procedural context (accuracy of record)
- **CMO** dated **3 June 2025** (served **8 June**).  
- **18 June 2025, 01:07** — I filed my **CMO-compliant updated disclosure list** and served it on the Respondent.  
- **19 September 2025, 16:51** — I notified **PH bundle omissions** and asked for insertion/re-pagination before the PH.  
- **23 September 2025, 08:49** — Respondent served a **same-day skeleton** “for use at the hearing today”.  
- **23 September 2025 (morning)** — I lodged a **same-day bundle/RA application** (bundle corrections + written-as-primary/paced participation). **No ruling** appears in the written reasons.

## B. Grounds (streamlined)

You’re saying:

* The **disciplinary hearing was on 12 Aug 2024 (only)** — not 7 Aug.
* A Judge has indicated your **evidence is weak** (esp. “no prior complaint/doctor report re anxiety/stress”), and is **considering strike-out** on the basis that your stress arose only as a **consequence of the disciplinary**.
* You insist your **statement already sets out when/how your condition began** and its effects. You want me to assess this **wearing Judge glasses** and anchor it in the **relevant law**.

Got it. Here’s a focused **JUDGE_MODE** analysis and an immediate plan to stop a strike-out.

---

# 1) Judge’s test for strike-out (ET Rules 2013, r.37) — where this really sits

* **Rule 37**: strike-out is only where a claim (or part) has **no reasonable prospect of success**.
* **Discrimination claims** are rarely suitable for strike-out: they usually require **fact-finding** and often **medical evidence**. A Rule 37 decision **is not** a mini-trial on disputed facts or medical causation.
* Practical judicial lens:

  * If there’s **any real factual dispute** (e.g., onset/recurrence; employer **knowledge** on/before **6 Aug 2024**; what adjustments were **available**; whether decisions were **because of** protected acts/traits), strike-out is **not appropriate**.
  * The proportionate course is a **preliminary issue** (e.g., disability) with **directions for medical evidence**, not strike-out.

**Ask the Judge now:** “Even if the current medical material is thin, the proper case management is a **preliminary issue on disability**, not Rule 37 strike-out.”

---

# 2) Disability in law (EqA 2010, s.6 & Schedule 1) — why ‘stress caused by discipline’ is the wrong test

* **Legal test**: a **mental impairment** with a **substantial** and **long-term** adverse effect on **normal day-to-day activities**.
* **Cause is not disqualifying**: It **doesn’t matter why** the impairment arose (work events, disciplinary, personal). The question is **what effects** it had and whether they were **substantial** and **long-term** (or **likely** to last 12 months / **likely** to **recur**).
* **Episodic/recurring conditions** (anxiety/depression) still qualify if effects are substantial and **likely to recur** (Schedule 1).
* **Timing**: assess “long-term” based on what was **known or could reasonably be expected** at the material time — not with hindsight only.

**So even if** symptoms intensified around the disciplinary, that **does not bar** disability. The question is: do your **MHIS + GP records** show **substantial** effects and **duration/likelihood**?

---

# 3) s.15 EqA (discrimination arising from disability) — why this still bites

* **Causation**: treatment “**arising in consequence of**” disability is a **loose causal link** (it need **not** be the only or main cause).
* **Knowledge**: the employer’s **knowledge of disability** is a **separate limb**; your **1 Aug 2024 MED3** and the **6 Aug** email acknowledgement are potent on this.
* **Justification**: the employer must show a **proportionate means** of achieving a **legitimate aim**. Proceeding to a **12 Aug** hearing during a **MED3** period, without **postponement / remote / written / OH**, is hard to justify unless they have a clear **paper trail** of reasons and rejected alternatives.

---

# 4) Reasonable Adjustments (ss.20–21) — keep it clinical and practical

* **PCP**: “Requirement to **attend/participate in a disciplinary hearing on 12 Aug 2024** while certified **not fit for work**, without **postponement**, **written submissions**, **CVP with timed breaks**, or **OH referral**.”
* If the Judge thinks evidence is thin, the proportionate step is: **order disclosure** of OH/adjustments consideration and (if still contested) list **RA** to be tried with disability — **not** strike-out.

---

# 5) Direct discrimination & Victimisation — should not be struck out with s.6 in dispute

* Even if disability is listed as a preliminary issue, your **direct discrimination (religion/sexual orientation)** and **victimisation** claims **do not require you to be disabled**.
* They turn on **comparators**, **remarks/patterns**, **difference in enforcement**, and **protected act (15 Aug 2024 appeal)** → **detriments**. These are **fact-heavy** and **unsuitable** for strike-out.

---

# 6) What I’d say to the Judge (short oral points — you can read these)

1. **Rule 37 threshold not met**: There is plainly a real dispute on disability (onset/recurrence/effects) and employer **knowledge by 6 Aug**. That requires **medical evidence** and **findings of fact**, not strike-out.
2. **Cause vs effect**: Whether stress escalated around discipline **does not answer** s.6 — the test is **effects and duration/likelihood**.
3. **s.15**: There is a real prospect that the **12 Aug** process **arose in consequence** of the condition and was **unjustified**, given the **1 Aug MED3** and the lack of documentary **adjustment consideration**.
4. **Case management**: If the Tribunal is uneasy about the medical record, the right order is a **preliminary issue on disability**, with **directions** for a **short clinician letter** and any **GP/CMHT records** (limited scope), not strike-out.
5. **Other claims**: **Direct discrimination** and **victimisation** are independent and should proceed.

---

- The **operative disclosure list** for the Preliminary Hearing was the **CMO-compliant** list submitted on **18 June 2025**, expressly “prepared pursuant to the CMO of 3 June” and “served in compliance with paragraph 25.”  
- Separately, on **30 April 2025** I made a **Rule 38/40** application concerning the **late ET3 / indulgence** (lodged **18:04**); the Tribunal granted indulgence at **18:28** and the Respondent filed its Amended ET3 at **18:56**.  
- The Written Reasons **do not address** my **30 April Rule 38/40** application at all, nor provide reasons on it. That omission is a **procedural irregularity** going to **fairness** and **equal footing**.

### Ground 2 — Same-day skeleton served at 08:49 for a 10:00 hearing, breaching Rule 38(2) (reasonable opportunity)  
- On the morning of the Preliminary Hearing (**23 September 2025**), the Respondent served a **skeleton argument at 08:49** asking that it be placed before the Judge for **use at the hearing that day (listed 10:00)**.  
- The skeleton advanced points including **strike-out/knock-out** on reasonable adjustments (PCP/disadvantage/adjustments).  
- I was afforded **no reasonable opportunity** to **reply in writing** or to **amend** in light of these points before the hearing began.  
- **Rule 38(2)** requires the Tribunal to ensure each party has a **reasonable opportunity** to present their case. The Written Reasons **do not grapple** with the timing/admission of the **08:49** skeleton or explain how fairness was preserved.

### Ground 3 — My request for reasonable adjustments (written submissions as primary mode, requested 7 August 2025) was never determined  
- I requested **reasonable adjustments** on **7 August 2025** (and renewed the request on the morning of the PH) that my **written submissions be the primary mode**, with **paced participation**.  
- The Written Reasons record minor facilitation on the day (e.g., a break and screen-share), but **do not determine** my core participation request for **written-as-primary**.  
- In the absence of a determination on participation, and with a **same-day skeleton** admitted, I was **not placed on an equal footing** and **not afforded a reasonable opportunity** to respond. This is a **procedural irregularity** under **Rule 3 / Rule 38(2)**.

These **three** discrete irregularities are **case-management errors** that **materially affected** the fairness of the disability determination:

> **(3)** If the application has not been refused under paragraph (2), the Tribunal must send a notice to the parties specifying the period by which any written representations in respect of the application must be received by the Tribunal, and seeking the views of the parties on whether the application can be determined without a hearing. The notice may also set out the Tribunal’s provisional views on the application.  
> **(4)** If the application has not been refused under paragraph (2), the judgment must be reconsidered at a hearing unless the Tribunal considers, having regard to any written representations provided under paragraph (3), that a hearing is not necessary in the interests of justice.

Short answer: I can’t find any place in the judge’s written reasons saying you were “preparing” your Mental Health Impact Statement during the PH. What the judge actually wrote is:

- She **applied the Wigginton sequence** for disability and then assessed your evidence. fileciteturn34file6L5-L13 fileciteturn34file6L17-L27

parts:
Short answer: **yes**—we’ve applied exactly under the **reconsideration** mechanism you’ve outlined. Two tiny housekeeping points on the rulebook:

- Since **6 Jan 2025**, the **Employment Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024 (SI 2024/1155)** are in force. Reconsideration now sits at **Rules 68–71** (Rule **70** is the screening/refusal gate). Substance is the same as the 2013 Rules. citeturn4search5turn1search6turn4search9
- The core principle remains: the Tribunal may reconsider **“where necessary in the interests of justice”**, and may **confirm, vary or revoke** the judgment. citeturn4search1

## What we’ve done (and why it fits Rule 68–71)
- **Filed in time**: Written reasons sent **1 Oct 2025** → 14-day window ends **15 Oct 2025**. Our draft is framed to clear **Rule 70(2)** (reasonable prospect). citeturn0search5  
- **Grounded in “interests of justice” / procedural irregularity** (not just disagreement with outcome):  
  1) **Participation RA not determined** (Rule 3/38 fairness angle).  
  2) **Outdated baseline + PH bundle omissions + 08:49 same-day skeleton** (no equal footing).  
  3) **Disability test misapplied** (effects/likely duration; MED3s understated).  
  4) **Adequacy of reasons (Rule 62 / _Meek_)**.  
  *(We also inserted your “top” add-ons: Grounds **9–13** and the practical relief asks.)*  
- **Process asks aligned to 70(3)–(4)**: short written-reps timetable; paper vs short hearing if needed. citeturn4search7

## Important reminder (appeal clock)
Applying for reconsideration **does not stop** the **42-day** EAT appeal clock. From **1 Oct 2025**, that points to **12 Nov 2025** for any **protective EAT appeal** if you want that safety net. citeturn0search2turn4search12

## Mini checklist (you’re good on these, but for completeness)
- **Send to** the Tribunal (cc Respondent).  
- **Attach** the annexes we listed (incl. **18 Jun** disclosure baseline, **19 Sep** bundle-omission email, **08:49** skeleton, **MED3s**, **EAP signpost**).  
- **Ask for** short **Rule 62** supplemental reasons on the four core points if the Tribunal prefers not to vary/revoke immediately. citeturn0search9

If you want, I can paste this confirmation plus the rule citations into the top of your Rule-70 draft in canvas so everything travels together.

Here’s a **judge-friendly, concise analysis** of the **Preliminary Hearing Written Reasons / Orders (23 Sep 2025)**, cross-referenced to the documents and to the legal rules/authorities in your Annex B. I’m not giving legal advice—just a clean read-across.

# Headline outcomes (PH, 23 Sep 2025)
- **Judge / Mode / Scope:** Employment Judge **Bradford**, Central London (video). Issues: disability status; list of issues; applications; directions/timetable. fileciteturn19file0L7-L19  
- **Para 7 / Disability stance & “EqA 2006” typo:** Respondent’s stance treated as **compliant** following a **varied date** (12→18 Aug); “EqA 2006” accepted as a typo; bar application **refused**. fileciteturn19file0L20-L37  
- **Disability (EqA 2010 s.6):** **Not disabled** at August 2024. Four-question sequence from **Wigginton** applied; **Igweike** quoted on evidential sufficiency; **Boyle** and **McDougall** applied on “long-term/likely” at material date. fileciteturn19file0L38-L49 fileciteturn19file0L50-L62 fileciteturn19file0L80-L90  
- **RA claim (EqA ss.20–21):** **Dismissed**—dependent on disability; no reasonable prospects. Separate short **Judgment** issued. fileciteturn19file0L91-L99 fileciteturn19file1L16-L27  
- **Deposit Order (Rule 40):** **£120 total (£30 per allegation)** for direct religion/belief, direct sexual orientation, wrongful dismissal, victimisation—each found to have **little reasonable prospect of success**. Means considered. fileciteturn19file2L19-L31 fileciteturn19file2L1-L9 fileciteturn19file2L63-L75  
- **Specific disclosure (Rule 31):** Ordered **within 7 days**: (a) comparator disciplinary records limited to smoking/parcel policies, (b) managers’ emails/messages re decision to invoke discipline, (c) policies on conflicts, smoking, EDI, discipline. Rest refused as **not relevant** to remaining issues. fileciteturn19file0L115-L133 fileciteturn19file0L134-L144  
- **List of issues & timetable:** Issues crystallised (wrongful dismissal; direct discrimination—religion/belief & sexual orientation; victimisation). **4-day** listing sufficient; witness/timetable split noted. fileciteturn19file0L100-L114 fileciteturn19file0L145-L165  
- **Promulgation/admin:** Orders/Judgment **sent 1 Oct 2025** (cover letter & email). fileciteturn19file3L28-L41 fileciteturn19file4L5-L19

# How the decision tracks the law (with cross-references)

## A) Disability decision (EqA 2010 s.6)
- **Framework used:** The judge expressly applied **Wigginton**’s four sequential questions (impairment → adverse effect → substantial → long-term). fileciteturn19file0L44-L62  
- **Evidence threshold:** Cites **Igweike** (Auerbach J)—claimant’s own account may be insufficient; adequacy is “practical/evidential,” sensitive to condition & proof. fileciteturn19file0L63-L79  
- **Long-term at the material date:** Applies **Boyle** (“could well happen”) and **McDougall** (assess **at date** of act). Finds symptoms tied to live disciplinary stress and **not likely** to be long-term. fileciteturn19file0L90-L99  
- **Outcome:** No disability in **Aug 2024**, so RA claim falls. fileciteturn19file0L98-L99

**Annex B alignment:** Your annex accurately flags **Rule 62** (reasons), and disability/RA principles; it cites **Rackham** and **Goodwin** on RA & adjustments, useful context for any participation adjustments—but here the judge made **in-hearing accommodations** (extra time; screen-share) and confined RA merits to the statutory dependency on disability. fileciteturn19file5L16-L29 fileciteturn19file0L38-L43

## B) Para 7 / Variation & bar application
- **Finding:** Tribunal treated the **deadline as varied to 18 Aug** and the “EqA 2006” as a **typo**; refused to **bar** the Respondent from contesting disability. fileciteturn19file0L28-L37  
- **Rule hooks:** Case-management discretion (Rules **3** & **31** context) and the live determination of disability at PH rather than by sanction. (See also Annex B on Rule 3 fairness and proportionate responses.) fileciteturn19file5L3-L11

## C) Deposit Order (Rule 40)
- **Test applied:** “**Little reasonable prospect of success**” for each allegation; judge took the case at its **highest**; no evidence heard. fileciteturn19file2L31-L43  
- **Comparators reasoning:** Smoking/vaping—admission vs. alleged breach by comparators; parcel process—different nature (no “intention to permanently deprive” for others). Hence **not materially the same circumstances**; hypothetical comparators may be required. fileciteturn19file2L43-L61 fileciteturn19file2L61-L71  
- **Reason for treatment:** CCTV inference + vaping admission likely explain the disciplinary process, undermining discriminatory causation. fileciteturn19file2L71-L83  
- **Victimisation & WD:** Victimisation—protected act/detriment may be arguable, but **causation** unlikely; wrongful dismissal likely falls if conduct reasons upheld. fileciteturn19file2L83-L99  
- **Means:** Monthly income/outgoings assessed; **£30 per claim** set with deterrent/affordability balance. fileciteturn19file2L99-L113

**Annex B alignment:** Your annex emphasises **Rule 39/40** and **means** proportionality (e.g., **Hemdan**). The judge’s reasons explicitly discuss means, consistent with that line. fileciteturn19file5L12-L19

## D) Specific disclosure (Rule 31)
- **Granted (targeted):** Comparators’ discipline (limited to smoking/parcel policies, with “no record” confirmations), internal decision-making emails, and core policy documents—**within 7 days**. fileciteturn19file0L115-L133  
- **Refused:** Wider categories as **not relevant** to remaining issues (post-withdrawal of unfair dismissal). Early targeted disclosure flagged to inform **deposit** decision. fileciteturn19file0L134-L144

**Annex C tie-in:** Your **Disclosure Matrix** maps closely to what was granted (comparators/policies/emails narrowed by relevance/proportionality), which supports the Rule 3 approach the judge adopted. fileciteturn19file6L1-L14 fileciteturn19file6L31-L40

# Clean “What this means (procedurally)”
- **Resolved at PH:** (1) **No disability** at August 2024; (2) **RA claim dismissed**; (3) **Deposit ordered** on four remaining allegations; (4) **Disclosure ordered** (narrow, 7 days); (5) **Issues listed** and **timetable** set. fileciteturn19file1L16-L27 fileciteturn19file2L19-L31 fileciteturn19file0L115-L133 fileciteturn19file0L145-L165  
- **Admin:** Orders/judgment **issued 1 Oct 2025**; cover letter sets **time limits** for written reasons, reconsideration (Rule 70), appeal (EAT). fileciteturn19file3L41-L62

Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

 
 

 

EMPLOYMENT TRIBUNALS 
 

Claimant:    Mr M Bagbozan 
  
Respondent:   The Co-operative Group Limited 

 
  

RECORD OF A PRELIMINARY HEARING 
  
Heard at: Central London, by video   On:   23 September 2025 
 
Before:  Employment Judge Bradford 
 
Appearances 
For the Claimant:   In person 
For the Respondent:   Miss A Bibi, Litigation Consultant 
 

 

1. This was a case management hearing listed to: 

a) Determine disability status 

b) Finalise the List of Issues 

c) Deal with any applications 

d) Review the length of the final hearing, witnesses to be called and timetable 

2. The Claimant had written to the Tribunal on 9 and 11 September 2024 stating 

that the Respondent had not complied with the Tribunal’s orders and 

requesting reasonable adjustments at this hearing. I therefore began by 

asking the Claimant what he wished the hearing to cover.  

3. The Claimant’s concerns were as follows: 

4. Firstly he considered that the Respondent’s email setting out its position 

regarding disability status did not comply with the rules. His concern was that 

the Tribunal had granted the Respondent’s application that the date for setting 

out its position be varied from 12 August 2025 to 18 August 2025, and that the 

email contained a typographical error in that it referred to the Equality Act 

2006, rather than 2010.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

5. Miss Bibi confirmed that the email should have referred to the 2010 Act, 

noting that there was no similar 2006 Act.  

6. I informed the Claimant that the Respondent had complied with the Tribunal’s 

case management order and served its position statement on the date 

required by the agreed extension. As disability was contested, I would be 

determining the issue today and I therefore would not be granting the 

Claimant’s application to bar the Respondent from contesting disability.  

7. The Claimant’s second concern was that the Respondent had twice requested 

extensions to the date for filing an amended response after the first case 

management hearing. It was clarified with Ms Bibi that the amended Grounds 

of Resistance were filed and sent to the Claimant on 30 April 2025, the date 

agreed by the Tribunal upon the Respondent’s second request for an 

extension of time. Whist the document appears to have been filed after 6pm, 

there was no time specified by the Tribunal and as such I could not say that 

the Respondent had failed to file the amended response in line with the 

extension granted. I would not be making a finding that the Respondent had 

failed to comply with an order.  

8. The Claimant confirmed that the reasonable adjustments he had requested 

related to this hearing, not the final hearing. He was given additional time to 

answer questions, permitted to screen share a document and given the time 

he needed to prepare of each part of the hearing in line with the requests he 

had made.  

Disability status  

9. Having heard submissions from the parties as to whether the Claimant had 

proved (the burden being on him) that he was a disabled person in 

accordance with section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024 (when the 

disciplinary proceedings took place) I determined that he was not. 

10. In accordance with Wigginton v Cowie and ors t/a Baxter International (A 

Partnership) EAT 0322/09 I asked myself four questions in sequential order: 

 

• did the claimant have a mental and/or physical impairment? (the 

‘impairment condition’) 

 

• did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out normal day-

to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

 

• was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial condition’), and 

 

• was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’). 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

11. The burden of proving disability rested on the Claimant. He had supplied an 

impact statement, however that was not supported by the medical records 

(nor was there any other evidence, such as Personal Independence 

Payments or similar).  

12. I had regard to the judgment of His Honour Judge Auerbach in Igweike v TSB 

Bank plc: ‘[I]t is a practical fact that, in some cases of this type, the individual’s 

own evidence may not be sufficient to satisfy the tribunal of the existence of 

an impairment... The question is a purely practical or evidential one, which is 

sensitive to the nature of the alleged disability, the facts, and the nature of the 

evidence, in the given case.’ 

Question 1 - Did the Claimant have a mental or physical impairment at the 

date he was undergoing disciplinary proceedings?  

13. The Claimant saw a doctor for the first time on 5 August 2024 and was signed 

off for 2 weeks, 1 – 15 August 2024, having cited stress at work and anxiety. 

No detail was given as to functional effects of condition on certificate. The 

doctor’s note of 5 August states that the Claimant reported that he had been 

under lot of stress working under difficult manager. He said he had been 

suspended, the doctor records the reason was unknown (although the 

Claimant had already attended the investigation interview). The Claimant 

reported that he missed a disciplinary hearing the previous Thursday. He had 

not been back at work since then but was planning to file a dispute. The 

doctor recorded that a long conversation took place about the situation at 

work. The doctor concluded “Emotionally not acutely distressed”. He “agreed” 

to issue a certificate for 2 weeks.  

14. Prev note is dated 23 July 24  when a reminder was sent that the Claimant 

was due an NHS health check. There are no earlier records where the 

Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his 

disability impact statement such as poor sleep, difficulty with personal care 

and household tasks.  

15. I find that first presentation with work related stress was 5 August 2024 and 

that the stress complained of was due to disciplinary process at work. This 

could be considered a mental impairment. 

Question 2 - Did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out 

normal day-to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

16. The consultation on 5 August 2024 does not suggest an adverse impact on 

day to day activities. 

17. Whilst the Claimant has provided an impact statement, according to which his 

symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting his role with the Co-op in 

October 2023, there was no evidence whatsoever to support this assertion.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

18. I find that had the Claimant suffered with difficulty with sleep and 

concentration, and an inability to care for himself from late 2023/early 2024 as 

asserts, he would have consulted his GP. He did not. I make this finding in 

part because he has been keen to seek assistance from September/October 

2024, albeit that the records do not suggest a condition that adversely impacts 

on his day to day activities.  

Question 3 - Was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial 

condition’) 

19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no 

evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from 

October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having 

a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries 

about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to 

support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find 

there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 

2024 – the time he needs to establish disability).  

Question 4 - Was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’) 

20. At the date of the disciplinary (12 August 2024 after 2 postponements 

because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work 

for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long 

term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with 

Boyle v SCA Packaging Ltd. I also take into account that how long an 

impairment is likely to last is something to be determined at the date of the 

alleged discriminatory act in accordance with McDougall v Richmond Adult 

Community Centre. Given the Claimant had not complained of any difficulties 

with day to day activities or even stress before he was told he was to attend a 

disciplinary hearing, I find that the likelihood was that any symptoms would 

resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded.  

21. It follows that I do not find that the Claimant had a disability as defined in 

section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024, when the disciplinary process 

took place.  

Reasonable Adjustment complaint 

22. The Claimant’s reasonable adjustment claim, which is dependent on him 

proving disability, is that he was required to attend a disciplinary hearing when 

he had been signed off as unfit for work. I therefore dismiss this claim. It has 

no reasonable prospects of success and cannot logically proceed in light of 

my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person. 

A separate judgment is issued accordingly. 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

List of issues 

23. The remaining issues in the claim, having made that decision are direct 

discrimination, victimisation and wrongful dismissal as set out below. This is 

the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines 

otherwise.  

Deposit Order 

24. Having discussed the merits of the issues with the parties, I proposed, of my 

own volition, to make a deposit order, as set out in rule 40 of the Employment 

Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024. Having heard submissions, I made such an 

order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The 

implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential 

liability for the Respondent’s costs. 

Claimant’s application for specific disclosure 

25. The Claimant wrote to the Tribunal on 9 April 2025 requesting specific 

disclosure. He asked me to deal with that application. I did so, finding that the 

majority of the requests were not for documents relevant to the remaining 

issues in the claim (the Claimant’s unfair dismissal claim having previously 

been withdrawn due to lack of two years’ service). 

26. I ordered that the Respondent disclose the following: 

a) Disciplinary records of the named comparators, redacted save for any 

matters relating to breaches to the smoking policy and parcel policy. In the 

event that these employees have no disciplinary record arising from these 

policies, records do not need to be disclosed and that position is to be 

confirmed in writing to the Claimant; 

b) Any emails and messages between managers about the decision to invoke 

the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; 

c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary 

policy. 

27. These documents are to be disclosed within 7 days of receipt of this decision.  

28. I determined that the remainder of the documentation requested in the 

Claimant’s email of 9 April 2025 was not relevant to the remaining matters in 

dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any 

event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to 

whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to 

pursue his claims.  

 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

Hearing duration and timetable 

29. The Respondent indicated it anticipates calling three witnesses. The Claimant 

indicated likewise. It was agreed that the remaining issues are narrow; the two 

direct discrimination claims arise from the same facts. The wrongful dismissal 

claim is very narrow, and likely dependent on the factual findings in relation to 

discrimination. The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, and hence 

separate facts, but again is narrow, there being a single asserted protected 

act and single asserted detriment.  

30. It was in consequence agreed that all the witnesses will be relatively short. It 

was agreed that the current 4 day listing will be sufficient to deal with the 

remaining claims. The following timetable was in principle agreed, subject to 

the views of the Tribunal hearing the case: 

Day 1 2 hours Reading and preliminary issues 

 2 hours Claimant’s evidence 

Day 2 1 hour Claimant’s evidence 

 4 hours Respondent’s evidence 

Day 3 1 hour Closing submissions 

 4 hours Tribunal deliberations 

Day 4 5 hours Judgment on liability and 
remedy if indicated 

 

The Issues 

The issues the Tribunal will decide are set out below: 

1. Wrongful dismissal / Notice pay 

1.1 What was the claimant’s notice period? 

1.2 Was the claimant paid for that notice period? 

1.3 If not, was the claimant guilty of gross misconduct? 

 

2. Direct religion/belief discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

2.1 The claimant is Muslim. 

2.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 

2.2.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

2.2.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

2.3 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the Tribunal 

will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania and Gaurunbhai 

(in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the parcel 

process). 

2.4 If so, was it because of religion? 

 

3. Direct sexual orientation discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

3.1 Did the respondent do the following things: 

3.1.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

3.1.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

3.2 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the 

Tribunal will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania, Layla and 

Gaurunbhai (in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the 

parcel process). 

3.3 If so, was it because of his sexual orientation? 

 

4. Victimisation (Equality Act 2010 section 27) 

4.1 Did the claimant do a protected act as follows: 

4.1.1 appeal against dismissal?  

4.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

4.2.1 reject his appeal? 

4.3 By doing so, did it subject the claimant to detriment? 

4.4 If so, was it because the claimant did a protected act?  

 

 

        

      Employment Judge Bradford 

      Date: 23 September 2025 

 

 

     ORDER SENT TO THE PARTIES ON 

   1 October 2025   

................................................................................. 

   M PARRIS   

................................................................................. 

     FOR THE TRIBUNAL OFFICE

Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

 
 

 

EMPLOYMENT TRIBUNALS 
 

Claimant:    Mr M Bagbozan 
  
Respondent:   The Co-operative Group Limited 

 
  

RECORD OF A PRELIMINARY HEARING 
  
Heard at: Central London, by video   On:   23 September 2025 
 
Before:  Employment Judge Bradford 
 
Appearances 
For the Claimant:   In person 
For the Respondent:   Miss A Bibi, Litigation Consultant 
 

 

1. This was a case management hearing listed to: 

a) Determine disability status 

b) Finalise the List of Issues 

c) Deal with any applications 

d) Review the length of the final hearing, witnesses to be called and timetable 

2. The Claimant had written to the Tribunal on 9 and 11 September 2024 stating 

that the Respondent had not complied with the Tribunal’s orders and 

requesting reasonable adjustments at this hearing. I therefore began by 

asking the Claimant what he wished the hearing to cover.  

3. The Claimant’s concerns were as follows: 

4. Firstly he considered that the Respondent’s email setting out its position 

regarding disability status did not comply with the rules. His concern was that 

the Tribunal had granted the Respondent’s application that the date for setting 

out its position be varied from 12 August 2025 to 18 August 2025, and that the 

email contained a typographical error in that it referred to the Equality Act 

2006, rather than 2010.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

5. Miss Bibi confirmed that the email should have referred to the 2010 Act, 

noting that there was no similar 2006 Act.  

6. I informed the Claimant that the Respondent had complied with the Tribunal’s 

case management order and served its position statement on the date 

required by the agreed extension. As disability was contested, I would be 

determining the issue today and I therefore would not be granting the 

Claimant’s application to bar the Respondent from contesting disability.  

7. The Claimant’s second concern was that the Respondent had twice requested 

extensions to the date for filing an amended response after the first case 

management hearing. It was clarified with Ms Bibi that the amended Grounds 

of Resistance were filed and sent to the Claimant on 30 April 2025, the date 

agreed by the Tribunal upon the Respondent’s second request for an 

extension of time. Whist the document appears to have been filed after 6pm, 

there was no time specified by the Tribunal and as such I could not say that 

the Respondent had failed to file the amended response in line with the 

extension granted. I would not be making a finding that the Respondent had 

failed to comply with an order.  

8. The Claimant confirmed that the reasonable adjustments he had requested 

related to this hearing, not the final hearing. He was given additional time to 

answer questions, permitted to screen share a document and given the time 

he needed to prepare of each part of the hearing in line with the requests he 

had made.  

Disability status  

9. Having heard submissions from the parties as to whether the Claimant had 

proved (the burden being on him) that he was a disabled person in 

accordance with section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024 (when the 

disciplinary proceedings took place) I determined that he was not. 

10. In accordance with Wigginton v Cowie and ors t/a Baxter International (A 

Partnership) EAT 0322/09 I asked myself four questions in sequential order: 

 

• did the claimant have a mental and/or physical impairment? (the 

‘impairment condition’) 

 

• did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out normal day-

to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

 

• was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial condition’), and 

 

• was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’). 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

11. The burden of proving disability rested on the Claimant. He had supplied an 

impact statement, however that was not supported by the medical records 

(nor was there any other evidence, such as Personal Independence 

Payments or similar).  

12. I had regard to the judgment of His Honour Judge Auerbach in Igweike v TSB 

Bank plc: ‘[I]t is a practical fact that, in some cases of this type, the individual’s 

own evidence may not be sufficient to satisfy the tribunal of the existence of 

an impairment... The question is a purely practical or evidential one, which is 

sensitive to the nature of the alleged disability, the facts, and the nature of the 

evidence, in the given case.’ 

Question 1 - Did the Claimant have a mental or physical impairment at the 

date he was undergoing disciplinary proceedings?  

13. The Claimant saw a doctor for the first time on 5 August 2024 and was signed 

off for 2 weeks, 1 – 15 August 2024, having cited stress at work and anxiety. 

No detail was given as to functional effects of condition on certificate. The 

doctor’s note of 5 August states that the Claimant reported that he had been 

under lot of stress working under difficult manager. He said he had been 

suspended, the doctor records the reason was unknown (although the 

Claimant had already attended the investigation interview). The Claimant 

reported that he missed a disciplinary hearing the previous Thursday. He had 

not been back at work since then but was planning to file a dispute. The 

doctor recorded that a long conversation took place about the situation at 

work. The doctor concluded “Emotionally not acutely distressed”. He “agreed” 

to issue a certificate for 2 weeks.  

14. Prev note is dated 23 July 24  when a reminder was sent that the Claimant 

was due an NHS health check. There are no earlier records where the 

Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his 

disability impact statement such as poor sleep, difficulty with personal care 

and household tasks.  

15. I find that first presentation with work related stress was 5 August 2024 and 

that the stress complained of was due to disciplinary process at work. This 

could be considered a mental impairment. 

Question 2 - Did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out 

normal day-to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

16. The consultation on 5 August 2024 does not suggest an adverse impact on 

day to day activities. 

17. Whilst the Claimant has provided an impact statement, according to which his 

symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting his role with the Co-op in 

October 2023, there was no evidence whatsoever to support this assertion.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

18. I find that had the Claimant suffered with difficulty with sleep and 

concentration, and an inability to care for himself from late 2023/early 2024 as 

asserts, he would have consulted his GP. He did not. I make this finding in 

part because he has been keen to seek assistance from September/October 

2024, albeit that the records do not suggest a condition that adversely impacts 

on his day to day activities.  

Question 3 - Was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial 

condition’) 

19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no 

evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from 

October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having 

a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries 

about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to 

support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find 

there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 

2024 – the time he needs to establish disability).  

Question 4 - Was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’) 

20. At the date of the disciplinary (12 August 2024 after 2 postponements 

because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work 

for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long 

term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with 

Boyle v SCA Packaging Ltd. I also take into account that how long an 

impairment is likely to last is something to be determined at the date of the 

alleged discriminatory act in accordance with McDougall v Richmond Adult 

Community Centre. Given the Claimant had not complained of any difficulties 

with day to day activities or even stress before he was told he was to attend a 

disciplinary hearing, I find that the likelihood was that any symptoms would 

resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded.  

21. It follows that I do not find that the Claimant had a disability as defined in 

section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024, when the disciplinary process 

took place.  

Reasonable Adjustment complaint 

22. The Claimant’s reasonable adjustment claim, which is dependent on him 

proving disability, is that he was required to attend a disciplinary hearing when 

he had been signed off as unfit for work. I therefore dismiss this claim. It has 

no reasonable prospects of success and cannot logically proceed in light of 

my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person. 

A separate judgment is issued accordingly. 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

List of issues 

23. The remaining issues in the claim, having made that decision are direct 

discrimination, victimisation and wrongful dismissal as set out below. This is 

the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines 

otherwise.  

Deposit Order 

24. Having discussed the merits of the issues with the parties, I proposed, of my 

own volition, to make a deposit order, as set out in rule 40 of the Employment 

Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024. Having heard submissions, I made such an 

order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The 

implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential 

liability for the Respondent’s costs. 

Claimant’s application for specific disclosure 

25. The Claimant wrote to the Tribunal on 9 April 2025 requesting specific 

disclosure. He asked me to deal with that application. I did so, finding that the 

majority of the requests were not for documents relevant to the remaining 

issues in the claim (the Claimant’s unfair dismissal claim having previously 

been withdrawn due to lack of two years’ service). 

26. I ordered that the Respondent disclose the following: 

a) Disciplinary records of the named comparators, redacted save for any 

matters relating to breaches to the smoking policy and parcel policy. In the 

event that these employees have no disciplinary record arising from these 

policies, records do not need to be disclosed and that position is to be 

confirmed in writing to the Claimant; 

b) Any emails and messages between managers about the decision to invoke 

the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; 

c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary 

policy. 

27. These documents are to be disclosed within 7 days of receipt of this decision.  

28. I determined that the remainder of the documentation requested in the 

Claimant’s email of 9 April 2025 was not relevant to the remaining matters in 

dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any 

event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to 

whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to 

pursue his claims.  

 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

Hearing duration and timetable 

29. The Respondent indicated it anticipates calling three witnesses. The Claimant 

indicated likewise. It was agreed that the remaining issues are narrow; the two 

direct discrimination claims arise from the same facts. The wrongful dismissal 

claim is very narrow, and likely dependent on the factual findings in relation to 

discrimination. The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, and hence 

separate facts, but again is narrow, there being a single asserted protected 

act and single asserted detriment.  

30. It was in consequence agreed that all the witnesses will be relatively short. It 

was agreed that the current 4 day listing will be sufficient to deal with the 

remaining claims. The following timetable was in principle agreed, subject to 

the views of the Tribunal hearing the case: 

Day 1 2 hours Reading and preliminary issues 

 2 hours Claimant’s evidence 

Day 2 1 hour Claimant’s evidence 

 4 hours Respondent’s evidence 

Day 3 1 hour Closing submissions 

 4 hours Tribunal deliberations 

Day 4 5 hours Judgment on liability and 
remedy if indicated 

 

The Issues 

The issues the Tribunal will decide are set out below: 

1. Wrongful dismissal / Notice pay 

1.1 What was the claimant’s notice period? 

1.2 Was the claimant paid for that notice period? 

1.3 If not, was the claimant guilty of gross misconduct? 

 

2. Direct religion/belief discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

2.1 The claimant is Muslim. 

2.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 

2.2.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

2.2.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

2.3 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the Tribunal 

will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania and Gaurunbhai 

(in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the parcel 

process). 

2.4 If so, was it because of religion? 

 

3. Direct sexual orientation discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

3.1 Did the respondent do the following things: 

3.1.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

3.1.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

3.2 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the 

Tribunal will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania, Layla and 

Gaurunbhai (in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the 

parcel process). 

3.3 If so, was it because of his sexual orientation? 

 

4. Victimisation (Equality Act 2010 section 27) 

4.1 Did the claimant do a protected act as follows: 

4.1.1 appeal against dismissal?  

4.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

4.2.1 reject his appeal? 

4.3 By doing so, did it subject the claimant to detriment? 

4.4 If so, was it because the claimant did a protected act?  

 

 

        

      Employment Judge Bradford 

      Date: 23 September 2025 

 

 

     ORDER SENT TO THE PARTIES ON 

   1 October 2025   

................................................................................. 

   M PARRIS   

................................................................................. 

     FOR THE TRIBUNAL OFFICE

there was no time specified by the Tribunal and as such I could not say that 

the Respondent had failed to file the amended response in line with the 

extension granted. I would not be making a finding that the Respondent had 

failed to comply with an order.  

8. The Claimant confirmed that the reasonable adjustments he had requested 

related to this hearing, not the final hearing. He was given additional time to 

answer questions, permitted to screen share a document and given the time 

he needed to prepare of each part of the hearing in line with the requests he 

had made.  

Disability status  

9. Having heard submissions from the parties as to whether the Claimant had 

proved (the burden being on him) that he was a disabled person in 

accordance with section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024 (when the 

disciplinary proceedings took place) I determined that he was not. 

10. In accordance with Wigginton v Cowie and ors t/a Baxter International (A 

Partnership) EAT 0322/09 I asked myself four questions in sequential order: 

 

• did the claimant have a mental and/or physical impairment? (the 

‘impairment condition’) 

 

• did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out normal day-

to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

 

• was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial condition’), and 

 

• was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’). 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

11. The burden of proving disability rested on the Claimant. He had supplied an 

impact statement, however that was not supported by the medical records 

(nor was there any other evidence, such as Personal Independence 

Payments or similar).  

12. I had regard to the judgment of His Honour Judge Auerbach in Igweike v TSB 

Bank plc: ‘[I]t is a practical fact that, in some cases of this type, the individual’s 

own evidence may not be sufficient to satisfy the tribunal of the existence of 

an impairment... The question is a purely practical or evidential one, which is 

sensitive to the nature of the alleged disability, the facts, and the nature of the 

evidence, in the given case.’ 

Question 1 - Did the Claimant have a mental or physical impairment at the 

date he was undergoing disciplinary proceedings?  

13. The Claimant saw a doctor for the first time on 5 August 2024 and was signed 

off for 2 weeks, 1 – 15 August 2024, having cited stress at work and anxiety. 

No detail was given as to functional effects of condition on certificate. The 

doctor’s note of 5 August states that the Claimant reported that he had been 

under lot of stress working under difficult manager. He said he had been 

suspended, the doctor records the reason was unknown (although the 

Claimant had already attended the investigation interview). The Claimant 

reported that he missed a disciplinary hearing the previous Thursday. He had 

not been back at work since then but was planning to file a dispute. The 

doctor recorded that a long conversation took place about the situation at 

work. The doctor concluded “Emotionally not acutely distressed”. He “agreed” 

to issue a certificate for 2 weeks.  

14. Prev note is dated 23 July 24  when a reminder was sent that the Claimant 

was due an NHS health check. There are no earlier records where the 

Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his 

disability impact statement such as poor sleep, difficulty with personal care 

and household tasks.  

15. I find that first presentation with work related stress was 5 August 2024 and 

that the stress complained of was due to disciplinary process at work. This 

could be considered a mental impairment. 

Question 2 - Did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out 

normal day-to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

16. The consultation on 5 August 2024 does not suggest an adverse impact on 

day to day activities. 

17. Whilst the Claimant has provided an impact statement, according to which his 

symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting his role with the Co-op in 

October 2023, there was no evidence whatsoever to support this assertion.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

18. I find that had the Claimant suffered with difficulty with sleep and 

concentration, and an inability to care for himself from late 2023/early 2024 as 

asserts, he would have consulted his GP. He did not. I make this finding in 

part because he has been keen to seek assistance from September/October 

2024, albeit that the records do not suggest a condition that adversely impacts 

on his day to day activities.  

Question 3 - Was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial 

condition’) 

19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no 

evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from 

October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having 

a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries 

about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to 

support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find 

there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 

2024 – the time he needs to establish disability).  

Question 4 - Was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’) 

20. At the date of the disciplinary (12 August 2024 after 2 postponements 

because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work 

for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long 

term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with 

Boyle v SCA Packaging Ltd. I also take into account that how long an 

impairment is likely to last is something to be determined at the date of the 

alleged discriminatory act in accordance with McDougall v Richmond Adult 

Community Centre. Given the Claimant had not complained of any difficulties 

with day to day activities or even stress before he was told he was to attend a 

disciplinary hearing, I find that the likelihood was that any symptoms would 

resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded.  

21. It follows that I do not find that the Claimant had a disability as defined in 

section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024, when the disciplinary process 

took place.  

Reasonable Adjustment complaint 

22. The Claimant’s reasonable adjustment claim, which is dependent on him 

proving disability, is that he was required to attend a disciplinary hearing when 

he had been signed off as unfit for work. I therefore dismiss this claim. It has 

no reasonable prospects of success and cannot logically proceed in light of 

my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person. 

A separate judgment is issued accordingly. 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

List of issues 

23. The remaining issues in the claim, having made that decision are direct 

discrimination, victimisation and wrongful dismissal as set out below. This is 

the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines 

otherwise.  

Deposit Order 

24. Having discussed the merits of the issues with the parties, I proposed, of my 

own volition, to make a deposit order, as set out in rule 40 of the Employment 

Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024. Having heard submissions, I made such an 

order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The 

implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential 

liability for the Respondent’s costs. 

Claimant’s application for specific disclosure 

25. The Claimant wrote to the Tribunal on 9 April 2025 requesting specific 

disclosure. He asked me to deal with that application. I did so, finding that the 

majority of the requests were not for documents relevant to the remaining 

issues in the claim (the Claimant’s unfair dismissal claim having previously 

been withdrawn due to lack of two years’ service). 

26. I ordered that the Respondent disclose the following: 

a) Disciplinary records of the named comparators, redacted save for any 

matters relating to breaches to the smoking policy and parcel policy. In the 

event that these employees have no disciplinary record arising from these 

policies, records do not need to be disclosed and that position is to be 

confirmed in writing to the Claimant; 

b) Any emails and messages between managers about the decision to invoke 

the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; 

c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary 

policy. 

27. These documents are to be disclosed within 7 days of receipt of this decision.  

28. I determined that the remainder of the documentation requested in the 

Claimant’s email of 9 April 2025 was not relevant to the remaining matters in 

dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any 

event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to 

whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to 

pursue his claims.  

 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

Hearing duration and timetable 

29. The Respondent indicated it anticipates calling three witnesses. The Claimant 

indicated likewise. It was agreed that the remaining issues are narrow; the two 

direct discrimination claims arise from the same facts. The wrongful dismissal 

claim is very narrow, and likely dependent on the factual findings in relation to 

discrimination. The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, and hence 

separate facts, but again is narrow, there being a single asserted protected 

act and single asserted detriment.  

30. It was in consequence agreed that all the witnesses will be relatively short. It 

was agreed that the current 4 day listing will be sufficient to deal with the 

remaining claims. The following timetable was in principle agreed, subject to 

the views of the Tribunal hearing the case: 

Day 1 2 hours Reading and preliminary issues 

 2 hours Claimant’s evidence 

Day 2 1 hour Claimant’s evidence 

 4 hours Respondent’s evidence 

Day 3 1 hour Closing submissions 

 4 hours Tribunal deliberations 

Day 4 5 hours Judgment on liability and 
remedy if indicated 

 

The Issues 

The issues the Tribunal will decide are set out below: 

1. Wrongful dismissal / Notice pay 

1.1 What was the claimant’s notice period? 

1.2 Was the claimant paid for that notice period? 

1.3 If not, was the claimant guilty of gross misconduct? 

 

2. Direct religion/belief discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

2.1 The claimant is Muslim. 

2.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 

2.2.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

2.2.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

2.3 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the Tribunal 

will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania and Gaurunbhai 

(in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the parcel 

process). 

2.4 If so, was it because of religion? 

 

3. Direct sexual orientation discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

3.1 Did the respondent do the following things: 

3.1.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

3.1.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

3.2 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the 

Tribunal will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania, Layla and 

Gaurunbhai (in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the 

parcel process). 

3.3 If so, was it because of his sexual orientation? 

 

4. Victimisation (Equality Act 2010 section 27) 

4.1 Did the claimant do a protected act as follows: 

4.1.1 appeal against dismissal?  

4.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

4.2.1 reject his appeal? 

4.3 By doing so, did it subject the claimant to detriment? 

4.4 If so, was it because the claimant did a protected act?  

 

 

        

      Employment Judge Bradford 

      Date: 23 September 2025 

 

 

     ORDER SENT TO THE PARTIES ON 

   1 October 2025   

................................................................................. 

   M PARRIS   

................................................................................. 

     FOR THE TRIBUNAL OFFICE
