No detail was given as to functional effects of condition on certificate. The 

doctor’s note of 5 August states that the Claimant reported that he had been 

under lot of stress working under difficult manager. He said he had been 

suspended, the doctor records the reason was unknown (although the 

Claimant had already attended the investigation interview). The Claimant 

reported that he missed a disciplinary hearing the previous Thursday. He had 

not been back at work since then but was planning to file a dispute. The 

doctor recorded that a long conversation took place about the situation at 

work. The doctor concluded “Emotionally not acutely distressed”. He “agreed” 

to issue a certificate for 2 weeks.  

14. Prev note is dated 23 July 24  when a reminder was sent that the Claimant 

was due an NHS health check. There are no earlier records where the 

Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his 

disability impact statement such as poor sleep, difficulty with personal care 

and household tasks.  

15. I find that first presentation with work related stress was 5 August 2024 and 

that the stress complained of was due to disciplinary process at work. This 

could be considered a mental impairment. 

Question 2 - Did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out 

normal day-to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

16. The consultation on 5 August 2024 does not suggest an adverse impact on 

day to day activities. 

17. Whilst the Claimant has provided an impact statement, according to which his 

symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting his role with the Co-op in 

October 2023, there was no evidence whatsoever to support this assertion.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

18. I find that had the Claimant suffered with difficulty with sleep and 

concentration, and an inability to care for himself from late 2023/early 2024 as 

asserts, he would have consulted his GP. He did not. I make this finding in 

part because he has been keen to seek assistance from September/October 

2024, albeit that the records do not suggest a condition that adversely impacts 

on his day to day activities.  

Question 3 - Was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial 

condition’) 

19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no 

evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from 

October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having 

a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries 

about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to 

support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find 

there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 

2024 – the time he needs to establish disability).  

Question 4 - Was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’) 

20. At the date of the disciplinary (12 August 2024 after 2 postponements 

because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work 

for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long 

term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with 

Boyle v SCA Packaging Ltd. I also take into account that how long an 

impairment is likely to last is something to be determined at the date of the 

alleged discriminatory act in accordance with McDougall v Richmond Adult 

Community Centre. Given the Claimant had not complained of any difficulties 

with day to day activities or even stress before he was told he was to attend a 

disciplinary hearing, I find that the likelihood was that any symptoms would 

resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded.  

21. It follows that I do not find that the Claimant had a disability as defined in 

section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024, when the disciplinary process 

took place.  

Reasonable Adjustment complaint 

22. The Claimant’s reasonable adjustment claim, which is dependent on him 

proving disability, is that he was required to attend a disciplinary hearing when 

he had been signed off as unfit for work. I therefore dismiss this claim. It has 

no reasonable prospects of success and cannot logically proceed in light of 

my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person. 

A separate judgment is issued accordingly. 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

List of issues 

23. The remaining issues in the claim, having made that decision are direct 

discrimination, victimisation and wrongful dismissal as set out below. This is 

the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines 

otherwise.  

Deposit Order 

24. Having discussed the merits of the issues with the parties, I proposed, of my 

own volition, to make a deposit order, as set out in rule 40 of the Employment 

Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024. Having heard submissions, I made such an 

order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The 

implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential 

liability for the Respondent’s costs. 

Claimant’s application for specific disclosure 

25. The Claimant wrote to the Tribunal on 9 April 2025 requesting specific 

disclosure. He asked me to deal with that application. I did so, finding that the 

majority of the requests were not for documents relevant to the remaining 

issues in the claim (the Claimant’s unfair dismissal claim having previously 

been withdrawn due to lack of two years’ service). 

26. I ordered that the Respondent disclose the following: 

a) Disciplinary records of the named comparators, redacted save for any 

matters relating to breaches to the smoking policy and parcel policy. In the 

event that these employees have no disciplinary record arising from these 

policies, records do not need to be disclosed and that position is to be 

confirmed in writing to the Claimant; 

b) Any emails and messages between managers about the decision to invoke 

the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; 

c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary 

policy. 

27. These documents are to be disclosed within 7 days of receipt of this decision.  

28. I determined that the remainder of the documentation requested in the 

Claimant’s email of 9 April 2025 was not relevant to the remaining matters in 

dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any 

event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to 

whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to 

pursue his claims.  

 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

Hearing duration and timetable 

29. The Respondent indicated it anticipates calling three witnesses. The Claimant 

indicated likewise. It was agreed that the remaining issues are narrow; the two 

direct discrimination claims arise from the same facts. The wrongful dismissal 

claim is very narrow, and likely dependent on the factual findings in relation to 

discrimination. The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, and hence 

separate facts, but again is narrow, there being a single asserted protected 

act and single asserted detriment.  

30. It was in consequence agreed that all the witnesses will be relatively short. It 

was agreed that the current 4 day listing will be sufficient to deal with the 

remaining claims. The following timetable was in principle agreed, subject to 

the views of the Tribunal hearing the case: 

Day 1 2 hours Reading and preliminary issues 

 2 hours Claimant’s evidence 

Day 2 1 hour Claimant’s evidence 

 4 hours Respondent’s evidence 

Day 3 1 hour Closing submissions 

 4 hours Tribunal deliberations 

Day 4 5 hours Judgment on liability and 
remedy if indicated 

 

The Issues 

The issues the Tribunal will decide are set out below: 

1. Wrongful dismissal / Notice pay 

1.1 What was the claimant’s notice period? 

1.2 Was the claimant paid for that notice period? 

1.3 If not, was the claimant guilty of gross misconduct? 

 

2. Direct religion/belief discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

2.1 The claimant is Muslim. 

2.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 

2.2.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

2.2.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

2.3 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the Tribunal 

will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania and Gaurunbhai 

(in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the parcel 

process). 

2.4 If so, was it because of religion? 

 

3. Direct sexual orientation discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

3.1 Did the respondent do the following things: 

3.1.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

3.1.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

3.2 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the 

Tribunal will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania, Layla and 

Gaurunbhai (in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the 

parcel process). 

3.3 If so, was it because of his sexual orientation? 

 

4. Victimisation (Equality Act 2010 section 27) 

4.1 Did the claimant do a protected act as follows: 

4.1.1 appeal against dismissal?  

4.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

4.2.1 reject his appeal? 

4.3 By doing so, did it subject the claimant to detriment? 

4.4 If so, was it because the claimant did a protected act?  

 

 

        

      Employment Judge Bradford 

      Date: 23 September 2025 

 

 

     ORDER SENT TO THE PARTIES ON 

   1 October 2025

   M PARRIS

Case No: 2225465/2024 

Preliminary hearing – deposit order and payment guidance note - rule 40.               
       

 
 

EMPLOYMENT TRIBUNALS 
 

 
Claimant:   Mr M Bagbozan 
 
Respondent:   The Co-operative Group Limited 
 
 
Heard at:  Central London (by video)  
 
On:   23 September 2025 
 
Before:  Employment Judge Bradford    
 
Representation 
Claimant:  In Person  
Respondent:  Ms A Bibi, Litigation Manager 
 
 

DEPOSIT ORDER 
 

 
The Employment Judge considers that the claimant’s allegations or arguments that he: 

• was discriminated against on the grounds of religion/belief;  

• was discriminated against due to sexual orientation; 

• was wrongfully dismissed; and  

• was victimised  
have little reasonable prospect of success.  The claimant is ORDERED to pay a deposit 
of £30/argument, totalling £120 not later than 21 days from the date this Order is sent as 
a condition of being permitted to continue to advance those allegations or arguments.  
The Judge has had regard to any information available as to the claimant’s ability to 
comply with the order in determining the amount of the deposit.   

 
 
 

REASONS 
 

1. Having heard submissions from both parties, I determined that each of the 
Claimant’s remaining claims has little reasonable prospect of success and 
as such, in accordance with rule 40 of the Employment Tribunal Procedure 
Rules 2024, I have made an order that £30 be paid in respect of each 
claim.  

2. In making this assessment I have conducted a broad assessment of the 
merits, taking the Claimant’s case at its highest. Whilst I have not heard 
any evidence, the documents before me including the pleadings indicate 



Case No: 2225465/2024 

Preliminary hearing – deposit order and payment guidance note - rule 40.               
       

that the broad facts are not in dispute, namely that the Claimant admitted 
to vaping contrary to the smoking policy, and that he in some way 
breached the parcel policy. 

3. The Claimant’s case is that being disciplined for these matters was 
unfavourable treatment due to either the protected characteristic of 
religion/belief or sexual orientation.  

4. Beginning with the direct discrimination claims, the Claimant’s cited 
comparators do not appear to have been in materially the same 
circumstances as him.  

5. With regard to vaping or smoking, the Respondent says that it has no 
evidence the policy was breached by the comparators. Whilst the Claimant 
may be able to prove otherwise, they cannot be people who admitted to 
breaching the smoking policy. The Respondent understood the Claimant 
made such an admission during the investigation meeting.  

6. As to the comparators the Claimant says also breached the parcel policy, 
the Respondent says that none of those people had been accused of an 
intention to permanently deprive the store of the contents of a parcel. This 
is what the Claimant was accused of. The (mis)conduct of others was 
therefore different in nature, and hence they were not in materially the 
same circumstances as the Claimant. 

7. It follows that the Tribunal is likely to use hypothetical comparators, and 
will need to decide whether such comparators would have been subject to 
the disciplinary process for the conduct alleged against the Claimant, or 
whether the disciplinary process was invoked in his case due to either 
religion/belief or sexual orientation.  

8. In the face of CCTV from which the Respondent inferred an intention on 
the Claimant’s part to take the contents of a parcel home (it is said that the 
footage shows him putting the contents of the parcel with his personal 
belongings), irrespective of whether that was his intention, the likelihood is 
that a Tribunal would find this was the reason for invoking the disciplinary 
policy. As the Respondent understood, from the Claimant’s responses in 
the investigation interview that he had admitted to vaping in breach of the 
smoking policy, again, the likelihood is that this will be found to be a 
reason for subjecting him to the disciplinary procedure.  

9. It will be for the Claimant to prove primary facts, which could lead a 
Tribunal to conclude, in the absence of any other explanation, that the 
reason for subjecting him to the disciplinary process was either 
religion/belief or sexual orientation. He has made no such link in his 
pleaded case. He made no such allegations prior to the disciplinary 
process being invoked. It follows that there is little reasonable prospect of 
his discrimination claims succeeding.  

10. The Claimant claims wrongful dismissal (notice pay). The Respondent 
says it dismissed him for gross misconduct and hence no notice pay was 
due. If the Claimant is unsuccessful in proving a discriminatory reason for 
the disciplinary process being invoked, it is likely the Tribunal will find that 
he was dismissed for gross misconduct and as such, this claim has little 
reasonable prospect of success.  



Case No: 2225465/2024 

Preliminary hearing – deposit order and payment guidance note - rule 40.               
       

11. Finally the Claimant claims victimisation. He says that the protected act 
was appealing his dismissal. The Respondent notes that he raised 
allegations of discrimination at that time, and a Tribunal may well find this 
to have been a protected act. A tribunal may also find that dismissing his 
appeal was a detriment. However, the Claimant is unlikely to establish that 
the reason his appeal was not upheld was because he had done a 
protected act, and likely to find that the Respondent had a genuine belief 
that he had committed gross misconduct. As such, this claim also has little 
reasonable prospect of success.  

12. I had regard to the Claimant’s ability to pay. He is in receipt of benefits in 
the sum of approximately £950/month. He stated his total income is 
£1,150. His rent (including bills) is £750 and he says he spends 
approximately £100/month on food. As such he has around £200/month 
disposable income. I therefore determined that £30/claim, totalling £120 is 
affordable, and also at a level that should encourage the Claimant to think 
carefully about whether he wishes to pursue these claims. He was 
informed of the likely cost liability in the event that his claims are 
unsuccessful for substantially the same reasons as set out above.  

  

      
     Employment Judge Bradford 
      
     Date: 23 September 2025 
 
      
 
     ORDER SENT TO THE PARTIES ON 
 

   1 October 2025

7. Payment of the deposit must be made by cheque or postal order only,

8. Payment should be accompanied by the tear-off slip below or should

9. Payment must be made to the address on the tear-off slip below.  
 
10. An acknowledgment of payment will not be issued, unless requested.

EMPLOYMENT TRIBUNALS


Case No: 2225465/2024 

Preliminary hearing – deposit order and payment guidance note - rule 40.               
       

 
 

EMPLOYMENT TRIBUNALS 
 

 
Claimant:   Mr M Bagbozan 
 
Respondent:   The Co-operative Group Limited 
 
 
Heard at:  Central London (by video)  
 
On:   23 September 2025 
 
Before:  Employment Judge Bradford    
 
Representation 
Claimant:  In Person  
Respondent:  Ms A Bibi, Litigation Manager 
 
 

DEPOSIT ORDER 
 

 
The Employment Judge considers that the claimant’s allegations or arguments that he: 

• was discriminated against on the grounds of religion/belief;  

• was discriminated against due to sexual orientation; 

• was wrongfully dismissed; and  

• was victimised  
have little reasonable prospect of success.  The claimant is ORDERED to pay a deposit 
of £30/argument, totalling £120 not later than 21 days from the date this Order is sent as 
a condition of being permitted to continue to advance those allegations or arguments.  
The Judge has had regard to any information available as to the claimant’s ability to 
comply with the order in determining the amount of the deposit.   

 
 
 

REASONS 
 

1. Having heard submissions from both parties, I determined that each of the 
Claimant’s remaining claims has little reasonable prospect of success and 
as such, in accordance with rule 40 of the Employment Tribunal Procedure 
Rules 2024, I have made an order that £30 be paid in respect of each 
claim.  

2. In making this assessment I have conducted a broad assessment of the 
merits, taking the Claimant’s case at its highest. Whilst I have not heard 
any evidence, the documents before me including the pleadings indicate 



Case No: 2225465/2024 

Preliminary hearing – deposit order and payment guidance note - rule 40.               
       

that the broad facts are not in dispute, namely that the Claimant admitted 
to vaping contrary to the smoking policy, and that he in some way 
breached the parcel policy. 

3. The Claimant’s case is that being disciplined for these matters was 
unfavourable treatment due to either the protected characteristic of 
religion/belief or sexual orientation.  

4. Beginning with the direct discrimination claims, the Claimant’s cited 
comparators do not appear to have been in materially the same 
circumstances as him.  

5. With regard to vaping or smoking, the Respondent says that it has no 
evidence the policy was breached by the comparators. Whilst the Claimant 
may be able to prove otherwise, they cannot be people who admitted to 
breaching the smoking policy. The Respondent understood the Claimant 
made such an admission during the investigation meeting.  

6. As to the comparators the Claimant says also breached the parcel policy, 
the Respondent says that none of those people had been accused of an 
intention to permanently deprive the store of the contents of a parcel. This 
is what the Claimant was accused of. The (mis)conduct of others was 
therefore different in nature, and hence they were not in materially the 
same circumstances as the Claimant. 

7. It follows that the Tribunal is likely to use hypothetical comparators, and 
will need to decide whether such comparators would have been subject to 
the disciplinary process for the conduct alleged against the Claimant, or 
whether the disciplinary process was invoked in his case due to either 
religion/belief or sexual orientation.  

8. In the face of CCTV from which the Respondent inferred an intention on 
the Claimant’s part to take the contents of a parcel home (it is said that the 
footage shows him putting the contents of the parcel with his personal 
belongings), irrespective of whether that was his intention, the likelihood is 
that a Tribunal would find this was the reason for invoking the disciplinary 
policy. As the Respondent understood, from the Claimant’s responses in 
the investigation interview that he had admitted to vaping in breach of the 
smoking policy, again, the likelihood is that this will be found to be a 
reason for subjecting him to the disciplinary procedure.  

9. It will be for the Claimant to prove primary facts, which could lead a 
Tribunal to conclude, in the absence of any other explanation, that the 
reason for subjecting him to the disciplinary process was either 
religion/belief or sexual orientation. He has made no such link in his 
pleaded case. He made no such allegations prior to the disciplinary 
process being invoked. It follows that there is little reasonable prospect of 
his discrimination claims succeeding.  

10. The Claimant claims wrongful dismissal (notice pay). The Respondent 
says it dismissed him for gross misconduct and hence no notice pay was 
due. If the Claimant is unsuccessful in proving a discriminatory reason for 
the disciplinary process being invoked, it is likely the Tribunal will find that 
he was dismissed for gross misconduct and as such, this claim has little 
reasonable prospect of success.  



Case No: 2225465/2024 

Preliminary hearing – deposit order and payment guidance note - rule 40.               
       

11. Finally the Claimant claims victimisation. He says that the protected act 
was appealing his dismissal. The Respondent notes that he raised 
allegations of discrimination at that time, and a Tribunal may well find this 
to have been a protected act. A tribunal may also find that dismissing his 
appeal was a detriment. However, the Claimant is unlikely to establish that 
the reason his appeal was not upheld was because he had done a 
protected act, and likely to find that the Respondent had a genuine belief 
that he had committed gross misconduct. As such, this claim also has little 
reasonable prospect of success.  

12. I had regard to the Claimant’s ability to pay. He is in receipt of benefits in 
the sum of approximately £950/month. He stated his total income is 
£1,150. His rent (including bills) is £750 and he says he spends 
approximately £100/month on food. As such he has around £200/month 
disposable income. I therefore determined that £30/claim, totalling £120 is 
affordable, and also at a level that should encourage the Claimant to think 
carefully about whether he wishes to pursue these claims. He was 
informed of the likely cost liability in the event that his claims are 
unsuccessful for substantially the same reasons as set out above.  

  

      
     Employment Judge Bradford 
      
     Date: 23 September 2025 
 
      
 
     ORDER SENT TO THE PARTIES ON 
 

   1 October 2025  
..................................................................................  

 
   M PARRIS  
.................................................................................. 

     FOR THE TRIBUNAL OFFICE

NOTE ACCOMPANYING DEPOSIT ORDER 

 

1. The Tribunal has made an order (a “deposit order”) requiring a party to 
pay a deposit as a condition of being permitted to continue to advance the 
allegations or arguments specified in the order.   

 
2. If that party pays the deposit and continues to advance the allegations or 

arguments specified in the order, but the Tribunal decides those 
allegations or arguments against that party for substantially the reasons 
given in the order, that party would then lose their deposit.  In addition, the 
Tribunal might make an award of costs or preparation time against that 
party for unreasonably pursuing those allegations or arguments. 

 
What happens if you do not pay the deposit?  
 

3. If the deposit is not paid the complaint or response to which the order 
relates will be struck out on the date specified in the order. 

 
When to pay the deposit? 

 
4. The party against whom the deposit order has been made must pay the 

deposit by the date specified in the order.    
 
5. If the deposit is not paid within that time, the complaint or response to 

which the order relates will be struck out. 
 

What happens to the deposit? 
 

6. If the Tribunal later decides the specific allegation or argument against the 
party which paid the deposit for substantially the reasons given in the 
deposit order, that party shall be treated as having acted unreasonably, 
unless the contrary is shown, and the deposit shall be paid to the other 
party (or, if there is more than one, to such party or parties as the Tribunal 
orders). If a costs or preparation time order is made against the party 
which paid the deposit, the deposit will go towards the payment of that 
order.  Otherwise, the deposit will be refunded. 
 
How to pay the deposit? 

 
7. Payment of the deposit must be made by cheque or postal order only, 

made payable to HMCTS. Payments CANNOT be made in cash. 
 
8. Payment should be accompanied by the tear-off slip below or should 

identify the Case Number and the name of the party paying the deposit. 
 
9. Payment must be made to the address on the tear-off slip below.  
 
10. An acknowledgment of payment will not be issued, unless requested.

11. Enquiries relating to the case should be made to the Tribunal office 

dealing with the case. 
 
12. Enquiries relating to the deposit should be referred to the address on the 

tear-off slip below or by telephone on 0117 930 2410.  The PHR 
Administration Team will only discuss the deposit with the party that has 
been ordered to pay the deposit.  If you are not the party that has been 
ordered to pay the deposit you will need to contact the Tribunal office 
dealing with the case. 

 
13. You have the right to appeal against the decision to make a deposit order 

if you consider that the decision, or the amount ordered, is wrong in law.  
The time for appealing is 42 days from the date on which the deposit order 
was sent out in writing by the Tribunal.  Details of how to appeal can be

Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

 
 

 

EMPLOYMENT TRIBUNALS 
 

Claimant:    Mr M Bagbozan 
  
Respondent:   The Co-operative Group Limited 

 
  

RECORD OF A PRELIMINARY HEARING 
  
Heard at: Central London, by video   On:   23 September 2025 
 
Before:  Employment Judge Bradford 
 
Appearances 
For the Claimant:   In person 
For the Respondent:   Miss A Bibi, Litigation Consultant 
 

 

1. This was a case management hearing listed to: 

a) Determine disability status 

b) Finalise the List of Issues 

c) Deal with any applications 

d) Review the length of the final hearing, witnesses to be called and timetable 

2. The Claimant had written to the Tribunal on 9 and 11 September 2024 stating 

that the Respondent had not complied with the Tribunal’s orders and 

requesting reasonable adjustments at this hearing. I therefore began by 

asking the Claimant what he wished the hearing to cover.  

3. The Claimant’s concerns were as follows: 

4. Firstly he considered that the Respondent’s email setting out its position 

regarding disability status did not comply with the rules. His concern was that 

the Tribunal had granted the Respondent’s application that the date for setting 

out its position be varied from 12 August 2025 to 18 August 2025, and that the 

email contained a typographical error in that it referred to the Equality Act 

2006, rather than 2010.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

5. Miss Bibi confirmed that the email should have referred to the 2010 Act, 

noting that there was no similar 2006 Act.  

6. I informed the Claimant that the Respondent had complied with the Tribunal’s 

case management order and served its position statement on the date 

required by the agreed extension. As disability was contested, I would be 

determining the issue today and I therefore would not be granting the 

Claimant’s application to bar the Respondent from contesting disability.  

7. The Claimant’s second concern was that the Respondent had twice requested 

extensions to the date for filing an amended response after the first case 

management hearing. It was clarified with Ms Bibi that the amended Grounds 

of Resistance were filed and sent to the Claimant on 30 April 2025, the date 

agreed by the Tribunal upon the Respondent’s second request for an 

extension of time. Whist the document appears to have been filed after 6pm, 

there was no time specified by the Tribunal and as such I could not say that 

the Respondent had failed to file the amended response in line with the 

extension granted. I would not be making a finding that the Respondent had 

failed to comply with an order.  

8. The Claimant confirmed that the reasonable adjustments he had requested 

related to this hearing, not the final hearing. He was given additional time to 

answer questions, permitted to screen share a document and given the time 

he needed to prepare of each part of the hearing in line with the requests he 

had made.  

Disability status  

9. Having heard submissions from the parties as to whether the Claimant had 

proved (the burden being on him) that he was a disabled person in 

accordance with section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024 (when the 

disciplinary proceedings took place) I determined that he was not. 

10. In accordance with Wigginton v Cowie and ors t/a Baxter International (A 

Partnership) EAT 0322/09 I asked myself four questions in sequential order: 

 

• did the claimant have a mental and/or physical impairment? (the 

‘impairment condition’) 

 

• did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out normal day-

to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

 

• was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial condition’), and 

 

• was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’). 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

11. The burden of proving disability rested on the Claimant. He had supplied an 

impact statement, however that was not supported by the medical records 

(nor was there any other evidence, such as Personal Independence 

Payments or similar).  

12. I had regard to the judgment of His Honour Judge Auerbach in Igweike v TSB 

Bank plc: ‘[I]t is a practical fact that, in some cases of this type, the individual’s 

own evidence may not be sufficient to satisfy the tribunal of the existence of 

an impairment... The question is a purely practical or evidential one, which is 

sensitive to the nature of the alleged disability, the facts, and the nature of the 

evidence, in the given case.’ 

Question 1 - Did the Claimant have a mental or physical impairment at the 

date he was undergoing disciplinary proceedings?  

13. The Claimant saw a doctor for the first time on 5 August 2024 and was signed 

off for 2 weeks, 1 – 15 August 2024, having cited stress at work and anxiety. 

No detail was given as to functional effects of condition on certificate. The 

doctor’s note of 5 August states that the Claimant reported that he had been 

under lot of stress working under difficult manager. He said he had been 

suspended, the doctor records the reason was unknown (although the 

Claimant had already attended the investigation interview). The Claimant 

reported that he missed a disciplinary hearing the previous Thursday. He had 

not been back at work since then but was planning to file a dispute. The 

doctor recorded that a long conversation took place about the situation at 

work. The doctor concluded “Emotionally not acutely distressed”. He “agreed” 

to issue a certificate for 2 weeks.  

14. Prev note is dated 23 July 24  when a reminder was sent that the Claimant 

was due an NHS health check. There are no earlier records where the 

Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his 

disability impact statement such as poor sleep, difficulty with personal care 

and household tasks.  

15. I find that first presentation with work related stress was 5 August 2024 and 

that the stress complained of was due to disciplinary process at work. This 

could be considered a mental impairment. 

Question 2 - Did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out 

normal day-to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

16. The consultation on 5 August 2024 does not suggest an adverse impact on 

day to day activities. 

17. Whilst the Claimant has provided an impact statement, according to which his 

symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting his role with the Co-op in 

October 2023, there was no evidence whatsoever to support this assertion.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

18. I find that had the Claimant suffered with difficulty with sleep and 

concentration, and an inability to care for himself from late 2023/early 2024 as 

asserts, he would have consulted his GP. He did not. I make this finding in 

part because he has been keen to seek assistance from September/October 

2024, albeit that the records do not suggest a condition that adversely impacts 

on his day to day activities.  

Question 3 - Was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial 

condition’) 

19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no 

evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from 

October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having 

a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries 

about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to 

support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find 

there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 

2024 – the time he needs to establish disability).  

Question 4 - Was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’) 

20. At the date of the disciplinary (12 August 2024 after 2 postponements 

because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work 

for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long 

term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with 

Boyle v SCA Packaging Ltd. I also take into account that how long an 

impairment is likely to last is something to be determined at the date of the 

alleged discriminatory act in accordance with McDougall v Richmond Adult 

Community Centre. Given the Claimant had not complained of any difficulties 

with day to day activities or even stress before he was told he was to attend a 

disciplinary hearing, I find that the likelihood was that any symptoms would 

resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded.  

21. It follows that I do not find that the Claimant had a disability as defined in 

section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024, when the disciplinary process 

took place.  

Reasonable Adjustment complaint 

22. The Claimant’s reasonable adjustment claim, which is dependent on him 

proving disability, is that he was required to attend a disciplinary hearing when 

he had been signed off as unfit for work. I therefore dismiss this claim. It has 

no reasonable prospects of success and cannot logically proceed in light of 

my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person. 

A separate judgment is issued accordingly. 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

List of issues 

23. The remaining issues in the claim, having made that decision are direct 

discrimination, victimisation and wrongful dismissal as set out below. This is 

the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines 

otherwise.  

Deposit Order 

24. Having discussed the merits of the issues with the parties, I proposed, of my 

own volition, to make a deposit order, as set out in rule 40 of the Employment 

Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024. Having heard submissions, I made such an 

order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The 

implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential 

liability for the Respondent’s costs. 

Claimant’s application for specific disclosure 

25. The Claimant wrote to the Tribunal on 9 April 2025 requesting specific 

disclosure. He asked me to deal with that application. I did so, finding that the 

majority of the requests were not for documents relevant to the remaining 

issues in the claim (the Claimant’s unfair dismissal claim having previously 

been withdrawn due to lack of two years’ service). 

26. I ordered that the Respondent disclose the following: 

a) Disciplinary records of the named comparators, redacted save for any 

matters relating to breaches to the smoking policy and parcel policy. In the 

event that these employees have no disciplinary record arising from these 

policies, records do not need to be disclosed and that position is to be 

confirmed in writing to the Claimant; 

b) Any emails and messages between managers about the decision to invoke 

the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; 

c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary 

policy. 

27. These documents are to be disclosed within 7 days of receipt of this decision.  

28. I determined that the remainder of the documentation requested in the 

Claimant’s email of 9 April 2025 was not relevant to the remaining matters in 

dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any 

event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to 

whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to 

pursue his claims.  

 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

Hearing duration and timetable 

29. The Respondent indicated it anticipates calling three witnesses. The Claimant 

indicated likewise. It was agreed that the remaining issues are narrow; the two 

direct discrimination claims arise from the same facts. The wrongful dismissal 

claim is very narrow, and likely dependent on the factual findings in relation to 

discrimination. The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, and hence 

separate facts, but again is narrow, there being a single asserted protected 

act and single asserted detriment.  

30. It was in consequence agreed that all the witnesses will be relatively short. It 

was agreed that the current 4 day listing will be sufficient to deal with the 

remaining claims. The following timetable was in principle agreed, subject to 

the views of the Tribunal hearing the case: 

Day 1 2 hours Reading and preliminary issues 

 2 hours Claimant’s evidence 

Day 2 1 hour Claimant’s evidence 

 4 hours Respondent’s evidence 

Day 3 1 hour Closing submissions 

 4 hours Tribunal deliberations 

Day 4 5 hours Judgment on liability and 
remedy if indicated 

 

The Issues 

The issues the Tribunal will decide are set out below: 

1. Wrongful dismissal / Notice pay 

1.1 What was the claimant’s notice period? 

1.2 Was the claimant paid for that notice period? 

1.3 If not, was the claimant guilty of gross misconduct? 

 

2. Direct religion/belief discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

2.1 The claimant is Muslim. 

2.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 

2.2.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

2.2.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

2.3 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the Tribunal 

will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania and Gaurunbhai 

(in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the parcel 

process). 

2.4 If so, was it because of religion? 

 

3. Direct sexual orientation discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

3.1 Did the respondent do the following things: 

3.1.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

3.1.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

3.2 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the 

Tribunal will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania, Layla and 

Gaurunbhai (in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the 

parcel process). 

3.3 If so, was it because of his sexual orientation? 

 

4. Victimisation (Equality Act 2010 section 27) 

4.1 Did the claimant do a protected act as follows: 

4.1.1 appeal against dismissal?  

4.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

4.2.1 reject his appeal? 

4.3 By doing so, did it subject the claimant to detriment? 

4.4 If so, was it because the claimant did a protected act?  

 

 

        

      Employment Judge Bradford 

      Date: 23 September 2025 

 

 

     ORDER SENT TO THE PARTIES ON 

   1 October 2025   

................................................................................. 

   M PARRIS   

................................................................................. 

     FOR THE TRIBUNAL OFFICE

evidence, in the given case.’

date he was undergoing disciplinary proceedings?  

13. The Claimant saw a doctor for the first time on 5 August 2024 and was signed 

off for 2 weeks, 1 – 15 August 2024, having cited stress at work and anxiety. 

No detail was given as to functional effects of condition on certificate. The 

doctor’s note of 5 August states that the Claimant reported that he had been 

under lot of stress working under difficult manager. He said he had been 

suspended, the doctor records the reason was unknown (although the 

Claimant had already attended the investigation interview). The Claimant 

reported that he missed a disciplinary hearing the previous Thursday. He had 

not been back at work since then but was planning to file a dispute. The 

doctor recorded that a long conversation took place about the situation at 

work. The doctor concluded “Emotionally not acutely distressed”. He “agreed” 

to issue a certificate for 2 weeks.  

14. Prev note is dated 23 July 24  when a reminder was sent that the Claimant 

was due an NHS health check. There are no earlier records where the 

Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his 

disability impact statement such as poor sleep, difficulty with personal care 

and household tasks.  

15. I find that first presentation with work related stress was 5 August 2024 and 

that the stress complained of was due to disciplinary process at work. This 

could be considered a mental impairment. 

Question 2 - Did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out 

normal day-to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

16. The consultation on 5 August 2024 does not suggest an adverse impact on 

day to day activities. 

17. Whilst the Claimant has provided an impact statement, according to which his 

symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting his role with the Co-op in 

October 2023, there was no evidence whatsoever to support this assertion.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

18. I find that had the Claimant suffered with difficulty with sleep and 

concentration, and an inability to care for himself from late 2023/early 2024 as 

asserts, he would have consulted his GP. He did not. I make this finding in 

part because he has been keen to seek assistance from September/October 

2024, albeit that the records do not suggest a condition that adversely impacts 

on his day to day activities.  

Question 3 - Was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial 

condition’) 

19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no 

evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from 

October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having 

a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries 

about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to 

support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find 

there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 

2024 – the time he needs to establish disability).

because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work 

for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long 

term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with

resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded.

my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person.

the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines 

otherwise.

order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The 

implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential

the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; 

c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary

dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any 

event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to 

whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to 

pursue his claims.

discrimination. The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, and hence 

separate facts, but again is narrow, there being a single asserted protected

2.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 

2.2.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location?

2.3 Was that less favourable treatment?

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference

would have been treated.

process).

parcel process).

4.1.1 appeal against dismissal?

Claim No: 2225465/2024

condition’) 

19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no 

evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from 

October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having 

a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries 

about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to 

support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find 

there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 

2024 – the time he needs to establish disability).  

Question 4 - Was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’) 

20. At the date of the disciplinary (12 August 2024 after 2 postponements 

because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work 

for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long 

term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with 

Boyle v SCA Packaging Ltd. I also take into account that how long an 

impairment is likely to last is something to be determined at the date of the 

alleged discriminatory act in accordance with McDougall v Richmond Adult 

Community Centre. Given the Claimant had not complained of any difficulties 

with day to day activities or even stress before he was told he was to attend a 

disciplinary hearing, I find that the likelihood was that any symptoms would 

resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded.  

21. It follows that I do not find that the Claimant had a disability as defined in 

section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024, when the disciplinary process 

took place.  

Reasonable Adjustment complaint 

22. The Claimant’s reasonable adjustment claim, which is dependent on him 

proving disability, is that he was required to attend a disciplinary hearing when 

he had been signed off as unfit for work. I therefore dismiss this claim. It has 

no reasonable prospects of success and cannot logically proceed in light of 

my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person. 

A separate judgment is issued accordingly. 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

List of issues 

23. The remaining issues in the claim, having made that decision are direct 

discrimination, victimisation and wrongful dismissal as set out below. This is 

the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines 

otherwise.  

Deposit Order 

24. Having discussed the merits of the issues with the parties, I proposed, of my 

own volition, to make a deposit order, as set out in rule 40 of the Employment 

Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024. Having heard submissions, I made such an 

order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The 

implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential 

liability for the Respondent’s costs. 

Claimant’s application for specific disclosure 

25. The Claimant wrote to the Tribunal on 9 April 2025 requesting specific 

disclosure. He asked me to deal with that application. I did so, finding that the 

majority of the requests were not for documents relevant to the remaining 

issues in the claim (the Claimant’s unfair dismissal claim having previously 

been withdrawn due to lack of two years’ service). 

26. I ordered that the Respondent disclose the following: 

a) Disciplinary records of the named comparators, redacted save for any 

matters relating to breaches to the smoking policy and parcel policy. In the 

event that these employees have no disciplinary record arising from these 

policies, records do not need to be disclosed and that position is to be 

confirmed in writing to the Claimant; 

b) Any emails and messages between managers about the decision to invoke 

the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; 

c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary 

policy. 

27. These documents are to be disclosed within 7 days of receipt of this decision.  

28. I determined that the remainder of the documentation requested in the 

Claimant’s email of 9 April 2025 was not relevant to the remaining matters in 

dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any 

event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to 

whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to 

pursue his claims.  

 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

Hearing duration and timetable 

29. The Respondent indicated it anticipates calling three witnesses. The Claimant 

indicated likewise. It was agreed that the remaining issues are narrow; the two 

direct discrimination claims arise from the same facts. The wrongful dismissal 

claim is very narrow, and likely dependent on the factual findings in relation to 

discrimination. The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, and hence 

separate facts, but again is narrow, there being a single asserted protected 

act and single asserted detriment.  

30. It was in consequence agreed that all the witnesses will be relatively short. It 

was agreed that the current 4 day listing will be sufficient to deal with the 

remaining claims. The following timetable was in principle agreed, subject to 

the views of the Tribunal hearing the case: 

Day 1 2 hours Reading and preliminary issues 

 2 hours Claimant’s evidence 

Day 2 1 hour Claimant’s evidence 

 4 hours Respondent’s evidence 

Day 3 1 hour Closing submissions 

 4 hours Tribunal deliberations 

Day 4 5 hours Judgment on liability and 
remedy if indicated 

 

The Issues 

The issues the Tribunal will decide are set out below: 

1. Wrongful dismissal / Notice pay 

1.1 What was the claimant’s notice period? 

1.2 Was the claimant paid for that notice period? 

1.3 If not, was the claimant guilty of gross misconduct? 

 

2. Direct religion/belief discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

2.1 The claimant is Muslim. 

2.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 

2.2.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

2.2.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

2.3 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the Tribunal 

will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania and Gaurunbhai 

(in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the parcel 

process). 

2.4 If so, was it because of religion? 

 

3. Direct sexual orientation discrimination (Equality Act 2010 section 13) 

3.1 Did the respondent do the following things: 

3.1.1 discipline him for smoking/vaping in an unauthorised location? 

3.1.2 discipline him for breach of the parcel process? 

3.2 Was that less favourable treatment? 

The Tribunal will decide whether the claimant was treated worse than 

someone else was treated. There must be no material difference 

between their circumstances and the claimant’s. 

If there was nobody in the same circumstances as the claimant, the 

Tribunal will decide whether they were treated worse than someone else 

would have been treated. 

The claimant says he was treated worse than Melania, Layla and 

Gaurunbhai (in respect of smoking) and Gaurunbhai (in respect of the 

parcel process). 

3.3 If so, was it because of his sexual orientation? 

 

4. Victimisation (Equality Act 2010 section 27) 

4.1 Did the claimant do a protected act as follows: 

4.1.1 appeal against dismissal?  

4.2 Did the respondent do the following things: 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

4.2.1 reject his appeal? 

4.3 By doing so, did it subject the claimant to detriment? 

4.4 If so, was it because the claimant did a protected act?  

 

 

        

      Employment Judge Bradford 

      Date: 23 September 2025

Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

 
 

 

EMPLOYMENT TRIBUNALS 
 

Claimant:    Mr M Bagbozan 
  
Respondent:   The Co-operative Group Limited 

 
  

RECORD OF A PRELIMINARY HEARING 
  
Heard at: Central London, by video   On:   23 September 2025 
 
Before:  Employment Judge Bradford 
 
Appearances 
For the Claimant:   In person 
For the Respondent:   Miss A Bibi, Litigation Consultant 
 

 

1. This was a case management hearing listed to: 

a) Determine disability status 

b) Finalise the List of Issues 

c) Deal with any applications 

d) Review the length of the final hearing, witnesses to be called and timetable 

2. The Claimant had written to the Tribunal on 9 and 11 September 2024 stating 

that the Respondent had not complied with the Tribunal’s orders and 

requesting reasonable adjustments at this hearing. I therefore began by 

asking the Claimant what he wished the hearing to cover.  

3. The Claimant’s concerns were as follows: 

4. Firstly he considered that the Respondent’s email setting out its position 

regarding disability status did not comply with the rules. His concern was that 

the Tribunal had granted the Respondent’s application that the date for setting 

out its position be varied from 12 August 2025 to 18 August 2025, and that the 

email contained a typographical error in that it referred to the Equality Act 

2006, rather than 2010.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

5. Miss Bibi confirmed that the email should have referred to the 2010 Act, 

noting that there was no similar 2006 Act.  

6. I informed the Claimant that the Respondent had complied with the Tribunal’s 

case management order and served its position statement on the date 

required by the agreed extension. As disability was contested, I would be 

determining the issue today and I therefore would not be granting the 

Claimant’s application to bar the Respondent from contesting disability.  

7. The Claimant’s second concern was that the Respondent had twice requested 

extensions to the date for filing an amended response after the first case 

management hearing. It was clarified with Ms Bibi that the amended Grounds 

of Resistance were filed and sent to the Claimant on 30 April 2025, the date 

agreed by the Tribunal upon the Respondent’s second request for an 

extension of time. Whist the document appears to have been filed after 6pm, 

there was no time specified by the Tribunal and as such I could not say that 

the Respondent had failed to file the amended response in line with the 

extension granted. I would not be making a finding that the Respondent had 

failed to comply with an order.  

8. The Claimant confirmed that the reasonable adjustments he had requested 

related to this hearing, not the final hearing. He was given additional time to 

answer questions, permitted to screen share a document and given the time 

he needed to prepare of each part of the hearing in line with the requests he 

had made.  

Disability status  

9. Having heard submissions from the parties as to whether the Claimant had 

proved (the burden being on him) that he was a disabled person in 

accordance with section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024 (when the 

disciplinary proceedings took place) I determined that he was not. 

10. In accordance with Wigginton v Cowie and ors t/a Baxter International (A 

Partnership) EAT 0322/09 I asked myself four questions in sequential order: 

 

• did the claimant have a mental and/or physical impairment? (the 

‘impairment condition’) 

 

• did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out normal day-

to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

 

• was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial condition’), and 

 

• was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’). 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

11. The burden of proving disability rested on the Claimant. He had supplied an 

impact statement, however that was not supported by the medical records 

(nor was there any other evidence, such as Personal Independence 

Payments or similar).  

12. I had regard to the judgment of His Honour Judge Auerbach in Igweike v TSB 

Bank plc: ‘[I]t is a practical fact that, in some cases of this type, the individual’s 

own evidence may not be sufficient to satisfy the tribunal of the existence of 

an impairment... The question is a purely practical or evidential one, which is 

sensitive to the nature of the alleged disability, the facts, and the nature of the 

evidence, in the given case.’ 

Question 1 - Did the Claimant have a mental or physical impairment at the 

date he was undergoing disciplinary proceedings?  

13. The Claimant saw a doctor for the first time on 5 August 2024 and was signed 

off for 2 weeks, 1 – 15 August 2024, having cited stress at work and anxiety. 

No detail was given as to functional effects of condition on certificate. The 

doctor’s note of 5 August states that the Claimant reported that he had been 

under lot of stress working under difficult manager. He said he had been 

suspended, the doctor records the reason was unknown (although the 

Claimant had already attended the investigation interview). The Claimant 

reported that he missed a disciplinary hearing the previous Thursday. He had 

not been back at work since then but was planning to file a dispute. The 

doctor recorded that a long conversation took place about the situation at 

work. The doctor concluded “Emotionally not acutely distressed”. He “agreed” 

to issue a certificate for 2 weeks.  

14. Prev note is dated 23 July 24  when a reminder was sent that the Claimant 

was due an NHS health check. There are no earlier records where the 

Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his 

disability impact statement such as poor sleep, difficulty with personal care 

and household tasks.  

15. I find that first presentation with work related stress was 5 August 2024 and 

that the stress complained of was due to disciplinary process at work. This 

could be considered a mental impairment. 

Question 2 - Did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out 

normal day-to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

16. The consultation on 5 August 2024 does not suggest an adverse impact on 

day to day activities. 

17. Whilst the Claimant has provided an impact statement, according to which his 

symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting his role with the Co-op in 

October 2023, there was no evidence whatsoever to support this assertion.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

18. I find that had the Claimant suffered with difficulty with sleep and 

concentration, and an inability to care for himself from late 2023/early 2024 as 

asserts, he would have consulted his GP. He did not. I make this finding in 

part because he has been keen to seek assistance from September/October 

2024, albeit that the records do not suggest a condition that adversely impacts 

on his day to day activities.  

Question 3 - Was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial 

condition’) 

19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no 

evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from 

October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having 

a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries 

about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to 

support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find 

there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 

2024 – the time he needs to establish disability).  

Question 4 - Was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’) 

20. At the date of the disciplinary (12 August 2024 after 2 postponements 

because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work 

for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long 

term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with 

Boyle v SCA Packaging Ltd. I also take into account that how long an 

impairment is likely to last is something to be determined at the date of the 

alleged discriminatory act in accordance with McDougall v Richmond Adult 

Community Centre. Given the Claimant had not complained of any difficulties 

with day to day activities or even stress before he was told he was to attend a 

disciplinary hearing, I find that the likelihood was that any symptoms would 

resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded.  

21. It follows that I do not find that the Claimant had a disability as defined in 

section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024, when the disciplinary process 

took place.  

Reasonable Adjustment complaint 

22. The Claimant’s reasonable adjustment claim, which is dependent on him 

proving disability, is that he was required to attend a disciplinary hearing when 

he had been signed off as unfit for work. I therefore dismiss this claim. It has 

no reasonable prospects of success and cannot logically proceed in light of 

my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person. 

A separate judgment is issued accordingly. 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

List of issues 

23. The remaining issues in the claim, having made that decision are direct 

discrimination, victimisation and wrongful dismissal as set out below. This is 

the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines 

otherwise.  

Deposit Order

own volition, to make a deposit order, as set out in rule 40 of the Employment 

Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024. Having heard submissions, I made such an 

order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The 

implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential 

liability for the Respondent’s costs. 

Claimant’s application for specific disclosure 

25. The Claimant wrote to the Tribunal on 9 April 2025 requesting specific 

disclosure. He asked me to deal with that application. I did so, finding that the 

majority of the requests were not for documents relevant to the remaining 

issues in the claim (the Claimant’s unfair dismissal claim having previously 

been withdrawn due to lack of two years’ service). 

26. I ordered that the Respondent disclose the following: 

a) Disciplinary records of the named comparators, redacted save for any 

matters relating to breaches to the smoking policy and parcel policy. In the 

event that these employees have no disciplinary record arising from these 

policies, records do not need to be disclosed and that position is to be 

confirmed in writing to the Claimant; 

b) Any emails and messages between managers about the decision to invoke 

the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; 

c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary 

policy. 

27. These documents are to be disclosed within 7 days of receipt of this decision.  

28. I determined that the remainder of the documentation requested in the

dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any 

event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to 

whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to 

pursue his claims.  

 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024

29. The Respondent indicated it anticipates calling three witnesses. The Claimant 

indicated likewise. It was agreed that the remaining issues are narrow; the two

claim is very narrow, and likely dependent on the factual findings in relation to

Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

 
 

 

EMPLOYMENT TRIBUNALS 
 

Claimant:    Mr M Bagbozan 
  
Respondent:   The Co-operative Group Limited 

 
  

RECORD OF A PRELIMINARY HEARING 
  
Heard at: Central London, by video   On:   23 September 2025 
 
Before:  Employment Judge Bradford 
 
Appearances 
For the Claimant:   In person 
For the Respondent:   Miss A Bibi, Litigation Consultant 
 

 

1. This was a case management hearing listed to: 

a) Determine disability status 

b) Finalise the List of Issues 

c) Deal with any applications 

d) Review the length of the final hearing, witnesses to be called and timetable 

2. The Claimant had written to the Tribunal on 9 and 11 September 2024 stating 

that the Respondent had not complied with the Tribunal’s orders and 

requesting reasonable adjustments at this hearing. I therefore began by 

asking the Claimant what he wished the hearing to cover.  

3. The Claimant’s concerns were as follows: 

4. Firstly he considered that the Respondent’s email setting out its position 

regarding disability status did not comply with the rules. His concern was that 

the Tribunal had granted the Respondent’s application that the date for setting 

out its position be varied from 12 August 2025 to 18 August 2025, and that the 

email contained a typographical error in that it referred to the Equality Act 

2006, rather than 2010.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

5. Miss Bibi confirmed that the email should have referred to the 2010 Act, 

noting that there was no similar 2006 Act.  

6. I informed the Claimant that the Respondent had complied with the Tribunal’s 

case management order and served its position statement on the date 

required by the agreed extension. As disability was contested, I would be 

determining the issue today and I therefore would not be granting the 

Claimant’s application to bar the Respondent from contesting disability.  

7. The Claimant’s second concern was that the Respondent had twice requested 

extensions to the date for filing an amended response after the first case 

management hearing. It was clarified with Ms Bibi that the amended Grounds 

of Resistance were filed and sent to the Claimant on 30 April 2025, the date 

agreed by the Tribunal upon the Respondent’s second request for an 

extension of time. Whist the document appears to have been filed after 6pm, 

there was no time specified by the Tribunal and as such I could not say that 

the Respondent had failed to file the amended response in line with the 

extension granted. I would not be making a finding that the Respondent had 

failed to comply with an order.  

8. The Claimant confirmed that the reasonable adjustments he had requested 

related to this hearing, not the final hearing. He was given additional time to 

answer questions, permitted to screen share a document and given the time 

he needed to prepare of each part of the hearing in line with the requests he 

had made.  

Disability status  

9. Having heard submissions from the parties as to whether the Claimant had 

proved (the burden being on him) that he was a disabled person in 

accordance with section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024 (when the 

disciplinary proceedings took place) I determined that he was not. 

10. In accordance with Wigginton v Cowie and ors t/a Baxter International (A 

Partnership) EAT 0322/09 I asked myself four questions in sequential order: 

 

• did the claimant have a mental and/or physical impairment? (the 

‘impairment condition’) 

 

• did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out normal day-

to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

 

• was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial condition’), and 

 

• was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’). 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

11. The burden of proving disability rested on the Claimant. He had supplied an 

impact statement, however that was not supported by the medical records 

(nor was there any other evidence, such as Personal Independence 

Payments or similar).  

12. I had regard to the judgment of His Honour Judge Auerbach in Igweike v TSB 

Bank plc: ‘[I]t is a practical fact that, in some cases of this type, the individual’s 

own evidence may not be sufficient to satisfy the tribunal of the existence of 

an impairment... The question is a purely practical or evidential one, which is 

sensitive to the nature of the alleged disability, the facts, and the nature of the 

evidence, in the given case.’ 

Question 1 - Did the Claimant have a mental or physical impairment at the 

date he was undergoing disciplinary proceedings?  

13. The Claimant saw a doctor for the first time on 5 August 2024 and was signed 

off for 2 weeks, 1 – 15 August 2024, having cited stress at work and anxiety. 

No detail was given as to functional effects of condition on certificate. The 

doctor’s note of 5 August states that the Claimant reported that he had been 

under lot of stress working under difficult manager. He said he had been 

suspended, the doctor records the reason was unknown (although the 

Claimant had already attended the investigation interview). The Claimant 

reported that he missed a disciplinary hearing the previous Thursday. He had 

not been back at work since then but was planning to file a dispute. The 

doctor recorded that a long conversation took place about the situation at 

work. The doctor concluded “Emotionally not acutely distressed”. He “agreed” 

to issue a certificate for 2 weeks.  

14. Prev note is dated 23 July 24  when a reminder was sent that the Claimant 

was due an NHS health check. There are no earlier records where the 

Claimant complains of stress or anxiety or any symptoms he reports in his 

disability impact statement such as poor sleep, difficulty with personal care 

and household tasks.  

15. I find that first presentation with work related stress was 5 August 2024 and 

that the stress complained of was due to disciplinary process at work. This 

could be considered a mental impairment. 

Question 2 - Did the impairment affect the claimant’s ability to carry out 

normal day-to-day activities? (the ‘adverse effect condition’) 

16. The consultation on 5 August 2024 does not suggest an adverse impact on 

day to day activities. 

17. Whilst the Claimant has provided an impact statement, according to which his 

symptoms of anxiety began shortly after starting his role with the Co-op in 

October 2023, there was no evidence whatsoever to support this assertion.  



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

18. I find that had the Claimant suffered with difficulty with sleep and 

concentration, and an inability to care for himself from late 2023/early 2024 as 

asserts, he would have consulted his GP. He did not. I make this finding in 

part because he has been keen to seek assistance from September/October 

2024, albeit that the records do not suggest a condition that adversely impacts 

on his day to day activities.  

Question 3 - Was the adverse condition substantial? (the ‘substantial 

condition’) 

19. This means more than minor or trivial. I find it was not, because there is no 

evidence it was. The Claimant was seen by Lambeth Talking Therapies from 

October 2024. Initial work was around regaining sense of self and him having 

a more balanced view of himself. The second appointment discussed worries 

about the future. There is no evidence that the Claimant sought strategies to 

support his carrying out of daily activities, meaning that I have no basis to find 

there was a substantial effect on them (albeit that this was slightly after August 

2024 – the time he needs to establish disability).  

Question 4 - Was the adverse condition long term? (the ‘long-term condition’) 

20. At the date of the disciplinary (12 August 2024 after 2 postponements 

because the Claimant did not attend) the Claimant had been signed off work 

for a few days. I need to address whether the condition was likely to be long 

term, ‘likely’ being in interpreted as ‘could well happen’ in accordance with 

Boyle v SCA Packaging Ltd. I also take into account that how long an 

impairment is likely to last is something to be determined at the date of the 

alleged discriminatory act in accordance with McDougall v Richmond Adult 

Community Centre. Given the Claimant had not complained of any difficulties 

with day to day activities or even stress before he was told he was to attend a 

disciplinary hearing, I find that the likelihood was that any symptoms would 

resolve once the disciplinary process was concluded.  

21. It follows that I do not find that the Claimant had a disability as defined in 

section 6 Equality Act 2010 in August 2024, when the disciplinary process 

took place.  

Reasonable Adjustment complaint 

22. The Claimant’s reasonable adjustment claim, which is dependent on him 

proving disability, is that he was required to attend a disciplinary hearing when 

he had been signed off as unfit for work. I therefore dismiss this claim. It has 

no reasonable prospects of success and cannot logically proceed in light of 

my finding that the Claimant was not, at the relevant time, a disabled person. 

A separate judgment is issued accordingly. 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

List of issues 

23. The remaining issues in the claim, having made that decision are direct 

discrimination, victimisation and wrongful dismissal as set out below. This is 

the final list of issues unless the Tribunal at the final hearing determines 

otherwise.  

Deposit Order 

24. Having discussed the merits of the issues with the parties, I proposed, of my 

own volition, to make a deposit order, as set out in rule 40 of the Employment 

Tribunal Procedure Rules 2024. Having heard submissions, I made such an 

order, and a separate document sets out the details and reasons. The 

implications of the order were explained to the Claimant, including potential 

liability for the Respondent’s costs. 

Claimant’s application for specific disclosure 

25. The Claimant wrote to the Tribunal on 9 April 2025 requesting specific 

disclosure. He asked me to deal with that application. I did so, finding that the 

majority of the requests were not for documents relevant to the remaining 

issues in the claim (the Claimant’s unfair dismissal claim having previously 

been withdrawn due to lack of two years’ service). 

26. I ordered that the Respondent disclose the following: 

a) Disciplinary records of the named comparators, redacted save for any 

matters relating to breaches to the smoking policy and parcel policy. In the 

event that these employees have no disciplinary record arising from these 

policies, records do not need to be disclosed and that position is to be 

confirmed in writing to the Claimant; 

b) Any emails and messages between managers about the decision to invoke 

the disciplinary policy in the Claimant’s case; 

c) Policies relating to conflicts of interest, smoking, EDI and the disciplinary 

policy. 

27. These documents are to be disclosed within 7 days of receipt of this decision.  

28. I determined that the remainder of the documentation requested in the 

Claimant’s email of 9 April 2025 was not relevant to the remaining matters in 

dispute. The above would/should be disclosed via standard disclosure in any 

event, however early disclosure may assist the Claimant in his decision as to 

whether to pay the deposit I have ordered and hence whether to continue to 

pursue his claims.  

 

 



Claim No: 2225465/2024 
 

Hearing duration and timetable 

29. The Respondent indicated it anticipates calling three witnesses. The Claimant 

indicated likewise. It was agreed that the remaining issues are narrow; the two 

direct discrimination claims arise from the same facts. The wrongful dismissal 

claim is very narrow, and likely dependent on the factual findings in relation to 

discrimination. The victimisation complaint relates to the appeal, and hence 

separate facts, but again is narrow, there being a single asserted protected 

act and single asserted detriment.  

30. It was in consequence agreed that all the witnesses will be relatively short. It 

was agreed that the current 4 day listing will be sufficient to deal with the 

remaining claims. The following timetable was in principle agreed, subject to 

the views of the Tribunal hearing the case: 

Day 1 2 hours Reading and preliminary issues 

 2 hours Claimant’s evidence 

Day 2 1 hour Claimant’s evidence 

 4 hours Respondent’s evidence 

Day 3 1 hour Closing submissions 

 4 hours Tribunal deliberations 

Day 4 5 hours Judgment on liability and 
remedy if indicated 

 

The Issues
